  / sum by (version) (rate(pantry_requests_total[1m]))

# 3. p95 latency, per version (95% of requests were faster than this, in seconds)
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, version) (rate(pantry_request_seconds_bucket[5m])))

Read them once, slowly. rate(counter[1m]) turns an ever-growing counter into "per second, recently". sum by (version) collapses the Pods into one line per version, which is the whole point for a canary. The error rate divides a filtered rate by the total rate. The histogram query is the one people copy and paste, and that is fine: it says "take the latency buckets, find the value below which 95% of requests fall".

Those three queries are also the three panels on Pantry's dashboard, in monitoring/grafana-dashboard.json. kubectl top is still useful for "which Pod is eating memory"; Prometheus is for "how is the service behaving over time, and compared to yesterday".

The commands

# Install Prometheus, Grafana and the operator in one release (takes a few minutes on first pull)
helm install monitoring prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack --version 91.4.1 \
  --namespace monitoring --create-namespace \
  --set grafana.adminPassword=pantry --set alertmanager.enabled=false --set nodeExporter.enabled=false

# Tell Prometheus to scrape Pantry
kubectl apply -f monitoring/servicemonitor.yaml

# Open Prometheus (targets page: Status → Targets) and Grafana (admin / pantry)
kubectl port-forward -n monitoring svc/monitoring-kube-prometheus-prometheus 9090:9090
kubectl port-forward -n monitoring svc/monitoring-grafana 3000:80

# Ask Prometheus a question from the terminal
curl -s --data-urlencode 'query=sum by (version) (rate(pantry_requests_total[1m]))' http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query

# Still the right tool for "which Pod is heavy right now?"
kubectl top pod -l app=pantry

# Remove the stack
helm uninstall monitoring -n monitoring

Try it

  1. Install the stack and wait for the Pods:
   helm repo add prometheus-community https://prometheus-community.github.io/helm-charts
   helm repo update
   helm install monitoring prometheus-community/kube-prometheus-stack --version 91.4.1 --namespace monitoring --create-namespace --set grafana.adminPassword=pantry --set alertmanager.enabled=false --set nodeExporter.enabled=false
   kubectl get pods -n monitoring -w

Wait for prometheus-monitoring-kube-prometheus-prometheus-0 to show 2/2 Running. First-time image pulls can take several minutes.

  1. Point the sensor network at Pantry, generate some traffic, and check the target is up:
   kubectl apply -f monitoring/servicemonitor.yaml
   for i in $(seq 1 80); do curl -s -o /dev/null -H 'Host: pantry.localtest.me' localhost/; done
   kubectl port-forward -n monitoring svc/monitoring-kube-prometheus-prometheus 9090:9090 &
   sleep 40; curl -s 'http://localhost:9090/api/v1/targets?state=active' | grep -o '"job":"pantry"[^}]*"health":"up"' | head -3

Three up matches, one per Pantry Pod. If the list is empty, check that the Service carries the app: pantry label and a port named http; ServiceMonitors select on both.

  1. Ask the three questions:
   curl -s --data-urlencode 'query=sum by (version) (rate(pantry_requests_total[1m]))' http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query
   curl -s --data-urlencode 'query=histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, version) (rate(pantry_request_seconds_bucket[5m])))' http://localhost:9090/api/v1/query
   kill %1
   

   {"status":"success","data":{"result":[{"metric":{"version":"v1"},"value":[...,"0.3643"]}]}}
   {"status":"success","data":{"result":[{"metric":{"version":"v1"},"value":[...,"0.0047"]}]}}

About a third of a request per second, and 95% of them under five milliseconds. The error-rate query returns nothing yet, because v1 has produced no 5xx responses and Prometheus does not invent zero series. Run v2 (chapter 17's canary, or kubectl set image deploy/pantry web=pantry:v2) and it appears.

  1. Open the wall of screens and import Pantry's dashboard:
   kubectl port-forward -n monitoring svc/monitoring-grafana 3000:80 &

Browse to http://localhost:3000, log in as admin / pantry, choose Dashboards → New → Import, and upload monitoring/grafana-dashboard.json. Three panels: request rate, error rate, p95, each with one line per version. Leave it open. The next chapter is going to make the error-rate line move.

Gotchas

  • The Prometheus installed by kube-prometheus-stack only picks up ServiceMonitors carrying the label release: <release name>; without it your target never appears and nothing complains.
  • A rate() window shorter than two scrape intervals returns nothing at all: with 15-second scrapes, [10s] is empty and [30s] is the floor; [1m] is the sensible default.
  • Prometheus does not invent zero: a series for status="500" exists only after the first 500, so an error-rate panel is empty, not zero, until something fails.
  • A ServiceMonitor selects a Service port by name; an unnamed port means no scrape.

Then and now

You will see "Prometheus Operator", "kube-prometheus" and "kube-prometheus-stack" used as if they were three products; they are the controller, the manifests built on it, and the Helm chart that installs both. Old Maps tells the story.

Recall

  1. How does Prometheus get its data, and what does that mean when a target dies?
  2. What are the three queries, in words?
  3. What does a ServiceMonitor need to match, on the Service and on itself?
  4. Which tool answers "which Pod is heavy right now" and which answers "how is the service behaving over time"?
  5. In the city metaphor, what are Prometheus and Grafana?
Show answers
  1. It scrapes /metrics on a timer; a dead target stops appearing.
  2. Request rate, error rate, p95 latency, each per version.
  3. The Service's app label and a named port; the ServiceMonitor's release label.
  4. kubectl top for now; Prometheus for over time.
  5. The sensor network and the wall of screens.

What Maya learned

  • Prometheus scrapes /metrics from targets on a timer; a ServiceMonitor tells it which Services to scrape.
  • Request rate, error rate and p95 latency, each sum by (version), answer "is it healthy?" for any HTTP service.
  • Grafana turns those queries into a dashboard; kubectl top remains the tool for "which Pod is heavy right now".

…but

Maya can finally see. What she sees, when she looks at the deployment history, is that the cluster does not match the repository. Someone raised Pantry's replicas by hand on Tuesday. Shop's ConfigMap has a value nobody committed. Three engineers have kubectl applyed from three laptops and the only record is their shell history. The dashboard shows what is happening; nothing shows what is supposed to be happening.

Chapter 19 · Act III · 5 min readNobody Touches the City by Hand#

The problem

The repository says Pantry has three replicas. The cluster has five. The repository says v1; one Deployment in staging says v2. Shop's ConfigMap has a feature flag that exists nowhere in Git. Every one of these was a sensible change made by a sensible person with kubectl apply or kubectl edit from a laptop, and every one of them is invisible to everybody else.

Maya's own release process is a Slack message saying "deploying now". If the cluster died tomorrow, rebuilding it would mean reconstructing what was running from memory.

The dashboard from chapter 18 shows what the city is. What she wants is a way to say what the city should be, in one place, and have something enforce it. She has said those words before, in chapter 6, about Pods. Raj points that out.

The idea

GitOps is the practice of keeping the desired state of a cluster in a Git repository and running a controller that continuously makes the cluster match it. Git becomes the only way to change production: a pull request is the change, its review is the approval, the merge is the deployment, and git log is the audit trail. Rolling back is git revert. Nobody runs kubectl apply against production, because anything applied by hand is drift, and the controller puts it back.

Argo CD is the most widely used of those controllers. You install it and give it an Application: a Git repository, a path, a target revision, and a destination cluster and namespace. It clones the repository, renders what it finds (plain YAML, a Helm chart, or a Kustomize overlay), compares it with the cluster, and reports Synced or OutOfSync. With automated sync it applies the difference itself; selfHeal also reverts drift, and prune deletes what Git no longer has.

Think of the city plan in the archive. The plan is the law; inspectors walk the city continuously and make every building match it, and if someone knocks a wall through by hand, they rebuild it. To change a building, you change the plan, which records every change and who made it.

Remember it as: Git is the city plan, Argo CD is the inspector who makes the city match it, and nobody changes a building by hand.

The Application is one resource:

apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: pantry
  namespace: argocd
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/<you>/<this-repo>.git
    targetRevision: HEAD
    path: examples/pantry/gitops          # plain YAML; could be a chart or a kustomize overlay
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: default
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true                          # delete what Git no longer has
      selfHeal: true                       # undo changes made by hand

The alternative to know is Flux: the same job as a set of smaller controllers configured entirely by Kubernetes resources, with no UI. Argo CD's UI draws every Application as a tree, which is a good way to learn what a Deployment owns; Flux is leaner.

Argo CD Flux
Shape One control plane with UI, CLI and API Composable controllers, no UI (community dashboards exist)
Config Application resources (or the UI) GitRepository + Kustomization / HelmRelease
Drift Reports OutOfSync; self-heal optional Reconciles on an interval
Choose when You want to see the app tree and hand it to a wider team You want the smallest footprint and everything as YAML

Here the three previous chapters meet. The v2 canary goes out through Istio at ten percent; Prometheus's error-rate panel for v2 climbs; the fix is git revert of the commit that changed the tag, and within three minutes Argo CD has put v1 back. The dial, the sensor and the plan are one system.

The commands

# Install Argo CD (takes a minute or two); --server-side because one of its CRDs is too big for client-side apply
kubectl create namespace argocd
kubectl apply -n argocd --server-side -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v3.5.3/manifests/install.yaml
kubectl port-forward -n argocd svc/argocd-server 8443:443
kubectl get secret -n argocd argocd-initial-admin-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d

# Log the CLI in through the tunnel
argocd login localhost:8443 --username admin --insecure

# Register the Application (from the file, or with the CLI) and look at it
kubectl apply -f argocd/application.yaml
argocd app create pantry --repo https://github.com/<you>/<this-repo>.git --path examples/pantry/gitops --dest-server https://kubernetes.default.svc --dest-namespace default --sync-policy automated --self-heal
argocd app list
argocd app get pantry

# The kubectl-native way to see what applying a file would change (what Argo does continuously)
kubectl diff -f gitops/

# Sync now, show what differs, see the history, go back
argocd app sync pantry
argocd app diff pantry
argocd app history pantry
argocd app rollback pantry <id>

# Remove
argocd app delete pantry
kubectl delete -n argocd -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v3.5.3/manifests/install.yaml

Try it

This chapter needs a Git repository Argo CD can reach: fork this book's repository on GitHub and put its URL in argocd/application.yaml.

  1. Install Argo CD and log in:
   kubectl create namespace argocd
   kubectl apply -n argocd --server-side -f https://raw.githubusercontent.com/argoproj/argo-cd/v3.5.3/manifests/install.yaml
   kubectl wait -n argocd --for=condition=Available deploy/argocd-server --timeout=300s
   kubectl port-forward -n argocd svc/argocd-server 8443:443 &
   argocd login localhost:8443 --username admin --insecure --password "$(kubectl get secret -n argocd argocd-initial-admin-secret -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 -d)"

Open https://localhost:8443 in a browser for the UI (same credentials).

  1. Hand Argo CD the plan and watch it sync:
   kubectl apply -f argocd/application.yaml
   sleep 30; argocd app get pantry | grep -E 'Sync Status|Health Status'
   

   Sync Status:        Synced to  (81c6092)
   Health Status:      Healthy

argocd app get pantry also lists what it owns: both Deployments, both Services and the ConfigMap, each Synced and Healthy.

  1. Knock a wall through by hand and watch the inspector fix it:
   kubectl scale deploy/pantry --replicas=5
   sleep 3; kubectl get deploy pantry
   

   NAME     READY   UP-TO-DATE   AVAILABLE   AGE
   pantry   3/3     3            3           4m

With selfHeal on, the extra Pods were gone before the command returned. argocd app history pantry records nothing, because nothing in Git changed. The only way to have five replicas is to commit five replicas.

  1. Ship the canary the proper way, then revert it. Edit examples/pantry/gitops/deployment.yaml, change pantry:v1 to pantry:v2, commit and push, then watch Argo CD notice and act:
   git commit -am "pantry: try v2" && git push
   argocd app get pantry --refresh | grep 'Sync Status'
   sleep 60; argocd app get pantry | grep 'Sync Status'
   kubectl get deploy pantry -o jsonpath='{.spec.template.spec.containers[0].image}{"\n"}'
   curl -s -H 'Host: pantry.localtest.me' localhost/
   

   Sync Status:        OutOfSync from  (551fb85)
   Sync Status:        Synced to  (551fb85)
   pantry:v2
   Welcome to the Pantry (v2). You are visitor #15. Served by pantry-759dbdd485-5gfgg.

v2 is live, and a few of those curls will come back as a 500, because v2 is flaky on purpose. The Grafana panel from chapter 18 shows v2's error rate climbing toward 30%. That is the number the customer asked for, and it says no:

   git revert --no-edit HEAD && git push
   sleep 60; argocd app get pantry | grep 'Sync Status'
   curl -s -H 'Host: pantry.localtest.me' localhost/
   argocd app history pantry
   

   Sync Status:        Synced to  (c1c2573)
   Welcome to the Pantry (v1). You are visitor #18. Served by pantry-5784c9bc56-fcqt8.
   ID      DATE                           REVISION
   0       2026-09-19 09:07:09 +0100 BST   (81c6092)
   1       2026-09-19 09:09:21 +0100 BST   (551fb85)
   2       2026-09-19 09:09:51 +0100 BST   (c1c2573)

Nobody ran kubectl. The commit is the rollback, the history is the audit trail, and everyone can see both. (Argo CD polls Git every three minutes; argocd app sync pantry skips the wait, and a webhook makes it instant.)

Gotchas

  • Argo CD's install manifest must be applied with --server-side; client-side apply rejects the ApplicationSet CRD as too large and the applicationset controller crash-loops.
  • argocd app delete cascades by default and removes every resource the Application manages; use --cascade=false to forget the Application and keep the workload.
  • With selfHeal on, a kubectl hotfix during an incident is reverted within seconds; the fix has to go through Git, which is the point, and also the thing to remember at 3 a.m.
  • A private repository needs a credential registered in Argo CD before the Application is created, or creation fails with "repository not accessible".

Recall

  1. What does "GitOps" change about how production is modified?
  2. What five things does an Application name?
  3. What do prune and selfHeal each do?
  4. How is a bad release rolled back under GitOps?
  5. In the city metaphor, what are Git and Argo CD?
Show answers
  1. Git becomes the only way; a merge deploys and a revert rolls back.
  2. Repository, path, revision, destination cluster, destination namespace.
  3. prune deletes what Git removed; selfHeal reverts changes made by hand.
  4. git revert and let Argo CD sync.
  5. The city plan in the archive and the inspector who enforces it.

What Maya learned

  • GitOps keeps the cluster's desired state in Git and lets a controller make the cluster match it, so a merge is a deployment and a revert is a rollback.
  • An Argo CD Application names a repo, a path and a destination; automated sync with self-heal reverts anything changed by hand.
  • Istio limits the blast radius, Prometheus measures it, and Git plus Argo CD is how the decision is made and recorded.

…but

There is no but. The city runs itself. Maya's phone has not rung at 3 a.m. in a month, and when Shop's next canary goes wrong, the person on call reads a dashboard, reverts a commit, and goes back to sleep. Everything she needed was one concept at a time, each one because the last one had a crack in it. The Epilogue has the whole map.

kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp    # what just happened here

Answers

One line per Recall question, by chapter. Attempt the questions first.

It Works On My Machine

  1. An image is a read-only recipe; a container is a running instance cooked from it.
  2. docker images lists images; docker ps lists running containers.
  3. --rm deletes the container when it exits; not when you want its logs or files afterwards.
  4. Yes, the image stays until docker rmi.
  5. A dish cooked from the recipe card.

Write the Recipe Down

  1. So a code change does not invalidate the cached dependency layer.
  2. RUN executes at build time; CMD is what runs when a container starts.
  3. The exec form, and only if process 1 handles the signal; a shell at PID 1 swallows it.
  4. The tag used when none is given; nothing about freshness.
  5. One step of the recipe, cached if unchanged.

Memory and Neighbours

  1. In Docker-managed storage outside any container; it survives docker rm.
  2. Only user-defined networks have DNS for container names.
  3. Laptop port 8000 forwards to container port 8080; the right-hand side is the container.
  4. docker inspect.
  5. A serving hatch to the street.

Ship It

  1. Registry, namespace, repository, tag; registry defaults to Docker Hub, tag to latest.
  2. Only the final stage ships; the builder's 1.6 GB of tools stays behind.
  3. docker push; the name must include your registry namespace.
  4. Nothing in the image needs root, and a compromised process should not have it.
  5. The cookbook library.

The Whole Band

  1. Its hostname on the project network.
  2. Without the condition it waits for the container to start; with it, for the healthcheck to pass.
  3. docker compose down keeps volumes; down -v deletes them.
  4. The directory name.
  5. The dinner menu.

The Night It Fell Over

  1. Self-heal across machines, scale across machines, roll out without downtime.
  2. docker kill counts as you stopping it; /crash was the process dying on its own.
  3. What you want to be true; the orchestrator loops until reality matches it.
  4. No; Kubernetes runs the same images.
  5. Docker cooks one meal; Kubernetes runs the whole city.

Meet the City

  1. API server (front desk), etcd (records), scheduler (housing office), controller manager (inspectors).
  2. The kubelet on each node.
  3. kubectl config current-context.
  4. Self-healing: nothing commands anything; every part notices and acts, forever.
  5. A building, and the records room.

The Smallest Thing That Runs

  1. apiVersion, kind, metadata, spec; the cluster adds status.
  2. apply compares the file with the cluster and changes only differences.
  3. kubectl create deployment … --dry-run=client -o yaml.
  4. That it will not start until the init container has exited successfully.
  5. An apartment.

Someone Who Never Sleeps

  1. A ReplicaSet keeps N Pods alive; a Deployment manages ReplicaSets to roll out changes.
  2. By label selector.
  3. maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0.
  4. kubectl rollout undo deploy/<name>.
  5. The building manager who never sleeps.

A Number That Never Changes

  1. A stable name and IP for whichever Pods match a selector; the Service object outlives the Pods.
  2. kubectl get endpoints <svc>; empty means the selector matches nothing.
  3. Inside the cluster; any node's IP on a high port; the internet via a cloud load balancer.
  4. An Ingress controller; without one the rules do nothing.
  5. The phone number and the front gate.

Sticky Notes and the Locked Drawer

  1. Handling: Secrets can be encrypted at rest, gated by RBAC separately, and hidden by tooling. The data is just base64.
  2. Mounted files.
  3. kubectl get secret … -o jsonpath='{.data.KEY}' | base64 -d.
  4. Configuration moved out of the image into ConfigMaps and Secrets.
  5. The locked drawer.

Are You Alive?

  1. Readiness failure removes the Pod from the Service; liveness failure restarts the container.
  2. /livez for liveness (process only), /healthz for readiness (needs Redis), so a Redis outage does not restart Pantry.
  3. Requests to place Pods; limits to throttle CPU and kill on memory.
  4. kubectl top pod.
  5. The lease: what is promised, and the ceiling.

Memory That Survives, Again

  1. A PVC requests storage, a StorageClass provisions a PV to satisfy it, the Pod mounts the PVC.
  2. WaitForFirstConsumer binding; it binds when a Pod uses it. Not a fault.
  3. A stable name and its own claim that follows it.
  4. kubectl get pvc,pv.
  5. The rental request for a storage unit.

Districts, Key Cards and Rush Hour

  1. Names, quotas and permissions.
  2. kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n <ns> --as=system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>.
  3. CPU requests on the Pods and metrics-server in the cluster.
  4. A NetworkPolicy.
  5. A one-off contractor, a scheduled cleaner, one caretaker per building.

The Night It Fell Over, Again

  1. describe for Pending, ImagePullBackOff and OOMKilled; logs --previous for CrashLoopBackOff.
  2. At the bottom, oldest first.
  3. The manager replaces anything you patch on a Pod.
  4. kubectl get events --sort-by=.lastTimestamp.
  5. The scheduler, the registry, the previous log, the lease.

Old Maps

  1. The image and runtime formats; the image never depended on Docker, only the adapter did.
  2. A Compose file with a deploy: block for Swarm; a Deployment.
  3. 1.16; the selector.
  4. Helm 2's in-cluster server; Helm 3 removed it.
  5. The adapter that let the caretaker use Docker's oven, now retired.

The Landlord's Week

  1. cordon blocks new Pods; drain cordons and evicts the existing ones.
  2. The replacement had nowhere to go, so the PodDisruptionBudget refused the second eviction.
  3. Nothing moves Pods on its own; a rollout restart replaces them where there is room.
  4. Requests; a Pod without requests counts as zero, so the LimitRange supplies defaults.
  5. "No new tenants", "everyone out politely", and the minimum who must stay in.

Flat-Pack Furniture

  1. The box, the assembled piece in your flat, the options sheet.
  2. helm template.
  3. helm rollback <release> <revision>.
  4. When you own all the YAML and environments differ by a few lines.
  5. helm get values <release>.

A Concierge at Every Door

  1. mTLS, retries and timeouts, telemetry, traffic splitting; none in application code.
  2. Gateway is the door, VirtualService the signpost with weights, DestinationRule the named subsets.
  3. The weight values, in the VirtualService.
  4. It has no sidecar, and STRICT mode refuses plaintext.
  5. The concierge at the door.

The Control Room

  1. It scrapes /metrics on a timer; a dead target stops appearing.
  2. Request rate, error rate, p95 latency, each per version.
  3. The Service's app label and a named port; the ServiceMonitor's release label.
  4. kubectl top for now; Prometheus for over time.
  5. The sensor network and the wall of screens.

Nobody Touches the City by Hand

  1. Git becomes the only way; a merge deploys and a revert rolls back.
  2. Repository, path, revision, destination cluster, destination namespace.
  3. prune deletes what Git removed; selfHeal reverts changes made by hand.
  4. git revert and let Argo CD sync.
  5. The city plan in the archive and the inspector who enforces it.

Where to go next

The book stopped where a laptop stops. The next steps, one pointer each:

  • A real cluster. EKS, GKE and AKS run the control plane for you; the concepts are identical, the Ingress and StorageClass names change. Start with your cloud's "create cluster" quickstart, then kubectl config use-context into it and re-run chapter 8.
  • Operators. A controller you install that understands a specific application (a database, a certificate authority) and manages it from a custom resource. Prometheus Operator in chapter 18 was one. Try cert-manager next: it turns "I want a TLS certificate for this Ingress" into a resource.
  • CI that builds images. The book pushed images by hand. GitHub Actions or GitLab CI should docker build, docker push, and bump the tag in gitops/ on every merge; Argo CD does the rest. Search for "GitOps image updater".
  • Deeper Istio. Ambient mode, retries and timeouts, authorization policies, multi-cluster. The Istio docs' "Tasks" section is task-shaped like this book.
  • Alerting. Prometheus's alertmanager (switched off in chapter 18 to save memory) turns the error-rate query into a page. Turn it on and write one rule: v2 error rate above 5% for 5 minutes.
  • Reading the source of truth. kubectl explain covers every field; the Kubernetes docs' "Concepts" section is the long version of Act II, and now you know the map.

Thank you for reading. Delete the cluster when you are done:

kind delete cluster --name pantry

Part IV · 4 min readThe Manuals#

The story is over. Pantry runs, the city runs itself, and you know what every piece is for. This part is different: it is not a story, it has no characters, and it has no length limit. It is what you reach for when you sit down to write a Dockerfile, a Compose file or a Kubernetes manifest from a blank page, or when someone asks you to review one.

Read the story first. The manuals assume you know what an image, a volume, a Pod and a Service are, and they do not explain those again. What they add is everything the story's twelve-command budget kept out: why the order of two lines in a Dockerfile costs you four minutes on every build, why USER app gets your Pod rejected while USER 10001 does not, why your rollout drops requests even though every probe is green, and what a reviewer looks for before they approve.

Who they are for

You have finished the story, or you already use Docker and Kubernetes at work and want to stop copying files you do not fully understand. After a manual you should be able to write its golden file from memory, explain every line of it, and find what is wrong in someone else's.

How a manual chapter works

Every chapter has the same shape, so you can jump straight to the part you need.

The ladder. The chapter is a sequence of rungs, from the first thing everyone needs to the advanced thing only some teams need. Each rung shows a small file or command and then three lines:

  • Rule: the one sentence you could write in a review comment.
  • Why: the mechanism behind the rule. This is what makes it stick, and what lets you work out the cases the rule does not cover.
  • Trap: what goes wrong when you get it wrong, and how you would notice. Every trap was reproduced, and its symptom is written down.

You can stop climbing whenever the rungs stop being relevant to you. The first two or three rungs of every chapter are things everybody needs. The last ones are what make you the expert in the room.

Decide. Some chapters have a table for choices with no single right answer: slim or distroless, env vars or mounted files, Helm or Kustomize.

The golden file. One production-grade file that uses every rung, with a comment on every line. The Docker manual's golden files grow into one hardened Pantry Dockerfile and one Compose project. The Kubernetes manual's grow from a single Pod into a whole namespace, then into a Helm chart.

Review checklist. The rungs restated as checkboxes. Use it on your own files and on pull requests.

Spot the bug. A file that looks reasonable and has several problems in it. Find them before you open the answers. If you find them all, you have learned the chapter. If you miss one, the answer tells you which rung to reread.

Where the files live

Every file shown with a path above it is in examples/manual/, exactly as printed, and was built or applied on the versions in the front matter. Each chapter's folder has a VERIFY.md with the commands that were run and what came back, including the symptom of every trap. Docker examples use host port 8000 and up. The Kubernetes examples run on kind, a few of them on a three-node cluster (examples/manual/kind-multinode.yaml) so that spreading, draining and storage behave the way they do on a real cluster.

The map

The Docker manual

  1. Every Instruction: what each Dockerfile line does, and the ones to avoid
  2. ENTRYPOINT, CMD and PID 1: how your process starts, and why it does not stop
  3. Context and Cache: fast builds, small contexts, BuildKit mounts
  4. Multi-Stage Builds: one file for dev, test and prod; choosing a base
  5. Users and Permissions: non-root, numeric UIDs, read-only filesystems, capabilities
  6. Supply Chain and Secrets: pinning, build secrets, multi-platform, SBOMs and scanning
  7. Networks: bridges, DNS, publishing ports safely, internal networks
  8. Volumes: named, bind and tmpfs mounts, ownership, backups
  9. Compose: The File: services, environment, health-gated startup
  10. Compose: The Project: overrides, profiles, includes, secrets, watch, limits

The Kubernetes manual

  1. Reading Any Manifest: anatomy, labels, explain, dry runs and server-side apply
  2. The Pod Spec: command and args, env sources, init containers, native sidecars
  3. Security Context: non-root, read-only, capabilities, seccomp, Pod Security Standards
  4. Lifecycle and Rollouts: probes done right, graceful shutdown, rollout strategy, disruption budgets
  5. Resources and Placement: requests, limits, QoS, affinity, taints, topology spread
  6. Config and Secrets: env versus files, reloads, projected volumes, what Secrets do not protect
  7. Storage: emptyDir, claims and classes, access modes, StatefulSets
  8. Networking: Service types, headless Services, Gateway API, NetworkPolicy
  9. Identity and Access: ServiceAccounts, tokens, least-privilege RBAC
  10. Packaging: Helm and Kustomize: charts worth reusing, overlays, when to pick which
  11. Debugging: the triage order, ephemeral containers, DNS and policy problems

The Bridge maps every Docker concept from the first manual to the Kubernetes field or object that replaces it, and says what changes in meaning on the way.

Docker manual · 1 · 12 min readEvery Instruction#

In the story: the recipe card, one step per line · Write the Recipe Down

A Dockerfile has about eighteen instructions, and you will write six of them every day. This chapter covers all the ones you will meet. For each one it gives the rule a reviewer applies and the reason behind it, so that when someone hands you a Dockerfile you can say what every line does and which ones are wrong. Two instructions are big enough to get their own chapters: ENTRYPOINT and CMD are in D2, and USER is in D5. Here they appear only where they have to.

Every Dockerfile in this chapter starts from the same idea. Each instruction either changes the filesystem, which makes a new layer, or changes the image's configuration (environment, user, default command, metadata), which costs nothing at runtime. Knowing which kind a line is answers most questions about it.

Changes the filesystem (new layer) Changes the configuration only
RUN, COPY, ADD FROM (picks the starting point), WORKDIR*, ENV, ARG, LABEL, EXPOSE, USER, HEALTHCHECK, STOPSIGNAL, SHELL, ENTRYPOINT, CMD, VOLUME, ONBUILD

* WORKDIR creates the directory if it is missing, which adds a tiny layer the first time.

The ladder

Rung 1 The five lines

Almost every Dockerfile you write starts as these five instructions in this order: a base, a working directory, the files, the build step, the default command.

FROM names the image you build on. Every stage starts with one. WORKDIR sets the directory that every later RUN, COPY, CMD and ENTRYPOINT uses, creating it if needed. Use it instead of RUN cd /app, because a cd lasts only until the end of its own RUN line. COPY <src> <dest> copies from the build context, which is the directory you pass to docker build, not the directory the Dockerfile sits in. RUN executes a command at build time and saves the resulting filesystem as a layer. CMD is what runs when someone starts a container without naming a command.

docker build -t pantry-manual:d01-r1 -f rung1.Dockerfile ../../pantry
docker run --rm -d -p 8001:8080 pantry-manual:d01-r1 && curl -s localhost:8001/livez

Rule Start every Dockerfile from the five lines (FROM, WORKDIR, COPY, RUN, CMD), using absolute paths for WORKDIR and exec form (["…"]) for CMD.

Why Each line has one job. WORKDIR persists across instructions while cd does not, and COPY sources are resolved against the build context, so the image is reproducible from that directory alone.

Trap COPY ../shared/lib.py . fails with "not found", however the path looks from where you are standing. A build can only see inside its context. Move the file into the context or make the context bigger (docker build -f app/Dockerfile . from the parent).

Rung 2 ARG and ENV, and where each one is visible

ARG is a build-time variable that you set with --build-arg. ENV is an environment variable baked into the image that every container gets. They look alike, and they have different lifetimes.

Built with --build-arg APP_VERSION=v7:

#5 0.211 PY at build time: ''  APP_VERSION at build time: 'v7'
$ docker run --rm pantry-manual:d01-r2
PY= APP_VERSION= PANTRY_VERSION=v7

Three things happened. PY was used by FROM (the base really was python:3.12-slim) and is empty inside the stage. An ARG declared before the first FROM is visible only to FROM lines. To use it inside a stage, declare it again with a bare ARG PY after the FROM. APP_VERSION existed during the build and is gone in the container. PANTRY_VERSION survived because an ENV line copied it.

The scope rules in one list:

  • ARG before FROM: visible in FROM lines only. Redeclare it (ARG PY) inside each stage that needs it.
  • ARG inside a stage: visible from that line to the end of that stage. Every stage has its own.
  • ENV: visible from that line on, in this stage and in any stage built FROM this one, and in every container.
  • Both are visible in docker history (D6). Neither is the place for a password.

Rule Use ARG for build inputs and ENV for runtime settings. When a build input must reach runtime, copy it explicitly with ENV X=${X}.

Why ARG values live only for the build of their stage, and an ARG before FROM lives only for the FROM lines. ENV values are written into the image configuration and inherited.

Trap ARG VERSION=1.2 at the top of the file, then RUN echo $VERSION prints an empty line and nothing errors. You notice when a version string or download URL inside the image is blank. Redeclare ARG VERSION after FROM.

Rung 3 COPY, and the two cases where ADD is right

ADD does everything COPY does, plus two surprises. It unpacks local tar archives, and it downloads URLs.

/added:
notes.txt
/copied:
notes.tar.gz
/licenses:
flask.txt

The same notes.tar.gz arrived packed through COPY and unpacked through ADD. If the file had been a .tar.gz you meant to ship as is (a dataset, a backup), ADD would quietly have changed your image. The remote ADD with --checksum is the one form worth keeping. BuildKit downloads the file, checks its SHA-256, and fails the build if it does not match:

ERROR: failed to solve: digest mismatch sha256:489a8e11…07ea: sha256:0000…0000

COPY has useful flags of its own. --chown and --chmod set ownership and mode while copying (D5), --from copies out of another stage or image (D4), and --link puts the copied files in an independent layer that survives a base-image change without a rebuild (D3).

Rule Use COPY for everything local. Use ADD only to unpack a local archive on purpose, or to fetch a remote file with --checksum.

Why COPY does exactly one thing. ADD's extra behaviours depend on what the file is, so the same line does different things to different inputs.

Trap ADD https://…/tool.tar.gz /opt/ without --checksum downloads whatever the server sends today, and a remote archive is not unpacked (only local ones are). You notice when /opt/tool.tar.gz is sitting there unextracted, or when last month's build and today's differ. Add --checksum, or RUN curl … | sha256sum -c in a pipefail shell (rung 5).

Rung 4 EXPOSE and LABEL: configuration, not behaviour

EXPOSE 8080 records that the process listens on 8080. It does not open anything. Without -p, nothing reaches the container from the host. With -P, Docker publishes every exposed port on a random host port:

$ docker run -d --name d01e pantry-manual:d01-r4 ; docker port d01e
$ docker run -d --name d01p -P pantry-manual:d01-r4 ; docker port d01p
8080/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:55000

LABEL adds key/value metadata to the image configuration. Use the OCI keys (org.opencontainers.image.source, .revision, .version, .title, .description, .licenses). Registries show them, scanners and Renovate read source to link an image to its repository, and docker inspect prints them. Group them in one LABEL instruction to keep the configuration tidy.

Rule Write EXPOSE for every port the process listens on, and set the OCI LABELs, knowing neither changes what the container does.

Why Both write to the image configuration only. EXPOSE is read by -P, by humans and by tools. Publishing is always the runner's decision (-p, Compose ports, a Kubernetes Service).

Trap You see EXPOSE 8080 and expect curl localhost:8080 to work, and you get "connection refused" with the container running. docker port <name> shows what is really published, and an empty answer means nothing is.

Rung 5 SHELL and the pipe that hides failures

RUN in shell form (RUN some command) runs through /bin/sh -c. A shell reports the exit status of the last command in a pipe, so a failing command on the left of | is invisible.

#5 3.661 ERROR: No matching distribution found for no-such-package-xyz
#6 0.201 the build carried on

pip failed, tail succeeded, and the build moved on. Switching the shell to bash with pipefail makes the whole pipe fail when any part of it does:

#5 ERROR: process "/bin/bash -o pipefail -c pip download no-such-package-xyz 2>&1 | tail -n 1" did not complete successfully: exit code: 1

SHELL changes the shell for every later shell-form RUN, CMD and ENTRYPOINT in the stage. Alpine has no bash. There, use SHELL ["/bin/ash", "-eo", "pipefail", "-c"], since busybox ash supports pipefail.

Long RUN lines read better as a heredoc, which BuildKit supports:

RUN <<EOF
set -eux
apt-get update
apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates
rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
EOF

set -e stops at the first failure, -u fails on unset variables, and -x prints each command in the build log.

Rule Put SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-o", "pipefail", "-c"] (or the ash equivalent) before any RUN that contains a pipe, and use set -eux in multi-line RUN heredocs.

Why A shell's exit status is that of the last command in a pipe, and BuildKit fails a step only on a non-zero exit status.

Trap RUN curl -fsSL $URL | tar -xz with a dead URL "succeeds" and leaves an empty directory. You find out at runtime, when the binary is missing. The build log shows curl's error a few lines above a step marked DONE.

Rung 6 HEALTHCHECK with what the image already has

HEALTHCHECK tells Docker how to test whether the process is working, not just running. docker ps then shows (healthy), (unhealthy) or (health: starting), and Compose can wait for healthy (D9).

The options:

  • --interval: time between checks.
  • --timeout: how long one check may take.
  • --start-period: a grace period during which failures do not count.
  • --retries: consecutive failures before the container is unhealthy.

The command must exit 0 for healthy and 1 for unhealthy.

The common mistake is the one in this file:

d01hg  Up 16 seconds (healthy)
d01hb  Up 17 seconds (unhealthy)
$ docker inspect -f '{{json (index .State.Health.Log 0).Output}}' d01hb
"/bin/sh: 1: curl: not found\n"

The app was fine. The check could not run, because -slim images do not ship curl. Use the language runtime the image already has, or a tiny static probe binary in distroless images.

Two limits are worth knowing. Docker only reports health. It does not restart an unhealthy container on its own (Compose's restart and Swarm do different things, D9). And Kubernetes ignores HEALTHCHECK completely, because it uses probes (K4).

Rule Write HEALTHCHECK in exec form, using only binaries the final image contains, with a --start-period that covers startup.

Why The check runs inside the container, so a missing tool fails every check. --start-period keeps a slow start from counting as failure.

Trap The container is unhealthy and the app answers fine. docker inspect -f '{{json .State.Health}}' <name> shows the check's own output, which is usually "not found" or a connection error to the wrong port.

Rung 7 VOLUME belongs to the runner, not the image

VOLUME /data in a Dockerfile tells Docker to mount a volume at /data in every container, and to create an anonymous one if the runner did not provide one.

$ docker run --rm pantry-manual:d01-r7
late.txt
seed.txt
volumes before=119 after two plain runs=121

Every docker run without --rm and without its own mount left behind a new anonymous volume, named by a 64-character hash, which nothing will ever reuse. On a CI machine that builds and runs tests a hundred times a day, that is a hundred volumes a day.

Notice late.txt. With BuildKit (the default builder since Docker Engine 23.0, 2023), a RUN after VOLUME keeps its changes. The legacy builder threw them away, which is why older advice says "never modify a path after declaring it a volume". The leak exists with either builder.

Rule Do not put VOLUME in application images. Let the runner mount storage (-v, Compose volumes, a Kubernetes volume, D8).

Why VOLUME cannot be undone by a child image or by the runner. Every container gets a volume at that path whether it wants one or not, and anonymous volumes outlive their containers unless removed with -v.

Trap docker volume ls shows hundreds of hash-named volumes and the disk fills up. docker volume ls -f dangling=true lists the orphans, and docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.Volumes}}' <image> shows which image declares them.

Rung 8 ONBUILD and other lines to recognise

ONBUILD <instruction> stores an instruction in the image and runs it when another Dockerfile uses this image as its FROM. It was popular for "builder" base images. You will meet it in old repositories, and you should not write it.

A child Dockerfile that says only FROM pantry-manual:d01-onbuild-base and CMD [...] fails with an error about a line it does not contain:

#6 [2/4] ONBUILD COPY requirements.txt .
ERROR: failed to solve: … "/requirements.txt": not found

Other lines to recognise and replace:

  • MAINTAINER name: deprecated. Use LABEL org.opencontainers.image.authors=….
  • STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT: which signal docker stop sends. D2 covers it.
  • # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1: the first line of a file, not an instruction. It pins the Dockerfile frontend to the latest stable 1.x, so features such as heredocs, --checksum and RUN --mount work on any BuildKit, whatever the daemon's own version.
  • # check=error=true: makes BuildKit's build checks fail the build instead of warning (see Decide).

Rule Do not write ONBUILD. Give child images explicit COPY and RUN lines, and start every Dockerfile with # syntax=docker/dockerfile:1.

Why ONBUILD triggers are invisible in the file you are reading (only docker inspect shows them). The syntax line makes features independent of the Docker version on the machine that builds.

Trap A build fails on COPY requirements.txt and your Dockerfile has no such line. docker inspect -f '{{json .Config.OnBuild}}' <base image> reveals the hidden steps.

Decide

You want to… Use Not
Copy local files COPY ADD
Unpack a local .tar.* into the image ADD file.tar.gz /dest/ COPY + RUN tar (an extra layer holding the archive)
Download a file at build time ADD --checksum=sha256:… <url> ADD <url> with no checksum
Pass a value into the build ARG + --build-arg ENV (it leaks into every container)
Configure the running app ENV (defaults), runtime -e / Compose / ConfigMap (real values) ARG (gone at runtime)
Pass a secret into the build RUN --mount=type=secret (D6) ARG or ENV (both readable in docker history)
Persistent data a mount chosen by the runner (D8) VOLUME in the image
Strict builds # check=error=true ignoring the warnings

BuildKit runs a set of build checks on every build and prints warnings such as JSONArgsRecommended (shell-form CMD), UndefinedVar and FromAsCasing. docker build --check . runs only the checks, and the # check=error=true directive under the syntax line turns warnings into failures. In CI, use the directive.

The golden file

Every instruction from the ladder, used the way a reviewer expects in a single-stage image. D4 splits it into stages, and D5 hardens it into the final golden Dockerfile.

docker build -t pantry-manual:d01 --build-arg PANTRY_VERSION=v3 -f Dockerfile ../../pantry
docker network create d01net
docker run -d --rm --name d01-redis --network d01net --network-alias redis redis:7-alpine
docker run -d --rm --name d01-web --network d01net -p 8001:8080 pantry-manual:d01
curl -s localhost:8001/           # Hello from Pantry (v3). You are visitor #1. …
docker ps --format '{{.Status}}'  # Up 14 seconds (healthy)

requirements-serve.txt is Pantry's own requirements.txt plus gunicorn, a production WSGI server. Flask's built-in server is for development, and it has no SIGTERM handler, which D2 shows matters.

Review checklist

Spot the bug

A Dockerfile from a pull request. It builds, and the container serves requests.

This file has 6 problems.

Show answers
  1. FROM python:latest is unpinned, and it is the full image. On the day of testing it resolved to Python 3.15.1 and produced a 1.66 GB image, against 205 MB for the golden file. Pin python:3.12-slim (and by digest, D6).
  2. ADD . . uses ADD where COPY is meant. Because it copies the whole context before installing dependencies, every code change reinstalls everything (D3), and Dockerfiles, gitops/ and old-maps/ ended up in the image. Copy requirements*.txt first and app.py after the install.
  3. pip install … | tee without pipefail hides a failed install. With flask==99.0.0 in requirements, pip printed "No matching distribution" and the build still produced an image. Add the SHELL line from rung 5, or drop the tee. pip also runs without --no-cache-dir, which leaves 1.9 MB of cache in the layer.
  4. VOLUME /app gives every container an anonymous volume over the code directory, and they pile up. Remove it.
  5. There is no USER, so the process runs as uid=0(root). Add a numeric non-root user (D5).
  6. CMD python app.py is shell form. /bin/sh is PID 1, the build prints JSONArgsRecommended, and docker stop waited the full 10 seconds before killing it. Use exec form with a server that handles SIGTERM (D2).

Docker manual · 2 · 10 min readENTRYPOINT, CMD and PID 1#

In the story: the dish the kitchen always makes, and the default order if nobody asks for anything else · Write the Recipe Down, The Night It Fell Over

Two lines decide how your container starts. Two facts about Linux decide whether it stops. Most "my container takes ten seconds to stop", "my arguments are ignored" and "Ctrl-C does nothing" problems come from one of these four things, and none of them shows up until you look.

The two lines are ENTRYPOINT and CMD. Docker glues them into one command line. The two facts are both about the first process in a container. It has process ID 1, and in Linux PID 1 is special in two ways. Signals it has no handler for are ignored instead of killing it, and it inherits every orphaned process in the container and is expected to reap them.

The ladder

Rung 1 Exec form and shell form

Both CMD and ENTRYPOINT (and RUN) come in two forms. Exec form is a JSON array, CMD ["python", "app.py"]. Docker runs that program directly, with those arguments. Shell form is plain text, CMD python app.py. Docker wraps it as /bin/sh -c "python app.py".

$ docker exec d02-shell cat /proc/1/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '
/bin/sh -c python app.py
$ time docker stop d02-shell
11s

The shell is PID 1. docker stop sends SIGTERM to the shell, the shell does not pass it to Python, and after ten seconds Docker gives up and sends SIGKILL. BuildKit warns about exactly this. The build prints JSONArgsRecommended: JSON arguments recommended for CMD to prevent unintended behavior related to OS signals.

Exec form has one limit: no shell means no variable expansion. CMD ["echo", "$HOME"] prints $HOME literally. When you need expansion, use an entrypoint script (rung 6), or CMD ["sh", "-c", "exec mytool --port \"$PORT\""] with an explicit exec.

Rule Write CMD and ENTRYPOINT in exec form, every time.

Why Exec form makes your program PID 1, so it receives signals directly. Shell form puts /bin/sh in front, and the shell does not forward them.

Trap docker stop always takes exactly ten seconds, and the exit code is 137 (128 + 9, killed). docker exec <name> cat /proc/1/cmdline shows /bin/sh -c … as PID 1.

Rung 2 ENTRYPOINT and CMD together

When both are set, Docker runs ENTRYPOINT followed by CMD. CMD becomes the default arguments, and docker run IMAGE args… replaces them. Measured on Alpine with echo:

ENTRYPOINT CMD docker run IMG docker run IMG x y
(none) ["echo","cmd"] cmd runs x y (here: "x: executable file not found")
["echo","ep"] (none) ep ep x y
["echo","ep"] ["cmd"] ep cmd ep x y
echo ep (shell) ["cmd"] ep ep
["echo","ep"] echo cmd (shell) ep /bin/sh -c echo cmd ep x y

Read the last two rows twice. A shell-form ENTRYPOINT swallows CMD and the run arguments: they become arguments to sh -c, which ignores them. A shell-form CMD under an exec-form ENTRYPOINT passes the literal words /bin/sh -c … as arguments.

So the useful patterns are:

  • Tool image: ENTRYPOINT ["mytool"] plus CMD ["--help"]. docker run img --version works naturally.
  • Service image: ENTRYPOINT ["docker-entrypoint.sh"] plus CMD ["server", "--flags"]. You can still run docker run img sh to debug (rung 6).
  • Simple image: CMD ["server", "--flags"] with no ENTRYPOINT. The whole command is replaceable.
ENTRYPOINT ["echo", "ep"]
CMD ["cmd"]

Rule Put what always runs in exec-form ENTRYPOINT and the overridable defaults in exec-form CMD, or use CMD alone.

Why Docker concatenates ENTRYPOINT + (docker run arguments, or else CMD). Only exec form keeps those arguments as separate words.

Trap docker run myimage --debug behaves exactly like docker run myimage. docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.Entrypoint}}' myimage shows a string wrapped in ["/bin/sh","-c",…], which is shell form.

Rung 3 Overriding at run time

Everything after the image name replaces CMD. --entrypoint replaces ENTRYPOINT, and it also clears CMD:

$ docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.Entrypoint}} {{json .Config.Cmd}}' pantry-manual:d02-t3
["echo","ep"] ["cmd"]
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint echo pantry-manual:d02-t3 overridden
overridden
$ docker run --rm --entrypoint echo pantry-manual:d02-t3
                                         ← empty: not "cmd"

--entrypoint takes a single executable, not a command line. --entrypoint "python -m pdb" fails. Use --entrypoint python IMG -m pdb app.py. Compose has the same two keys, entrypoint: and command: (D9), and Kubernetes calls them command: and args: (K2). Note that Kubernetes' command replaces ENTRYPOINT, not CMD. The Bridge chapter maps all of them.

docker run --rm --entrypoint sh pantry-manual:d02 -c 'id; ls /app'     # debug shell, bypassing the entrypoint
docker run --rm pantry-manual:d02 --version                             # arguments replace CMD only

Rule Override CMD with arguments after the image name, and use --entrypoint only to get a debugging shell, passing everything you need after the image.

Why --entrypoint resets CMD to empty by design, because the old defaults were written for the old entrypoint.

Trap docker run --entrypoint /usr/local/bin/myserver img starts with no flags at all and fails on "missing --config". The defaults you expected lived in CMD, which --entrypoint threw away.

Rung 4 PID 1 ignores signals it does not handle

Exec form is necessary, and it is not sufficient. Here is Pantry's Flask development server, in exec form:

$ docker exec d02-exec cat /proc/1/cmdline   →  python app.py
$ time docker stop d02-exec                  →  10s

Python is PID 1 now, and it still takes ten seconds. Normally SIGTERM's default action is "terminate". For PID 1 the kernel does not apply default actions: a signal is delivered only if the process installed a handler. Python installs a handler for SIGINT (it raises KeyboardInterrupt) but not for SIGTERM. That gives three fixes, each verified:

  1. Run a program that handles SIGTERM. gunicorn, nginx, the JVM, Node with a process.on('SIGTERM') handler, Go with signal.Notify. The D1 golden image stopped in 0.7 s.
  2. Tell Docker to send a signal it does handle. STOPSIGNAL SIGINT stopped the Flask server in under a second:
  1. Put a real init in front with --init (rung 5). It stopped in 1 s.

The best fix is the first one. A process that handles SIGTERM can finish in-flight requests, and the other two only make it die faster.

Rule Make sure PID 1 handles SIGTERM, preferably by running a server that drains on SIGTERM, otherwise with STOPSIGNAL or an init.

Why The kernel never applies a default signal action to a namespace's PID 1, so a signal without a handler is simply dropped.

Trap The command is in exec form and docker stop still takes the full timeout. Look for the exit code: 137 means it was killed, while 0 or 143 (128 + 15) means it exited on SIGTERM.

Rung 5 An init process, and zombies

PID 1 has a second job. When a process dies, its parent must call wait() to collect its exit status. Until then it is a zombie, an entry in the process table. When the parent dies first, the orphan is re-parented to PID 1, and PID 1 must reap it. A program that never expected to be PID 1 does not do this:

docker run -d --name z alpine:3.20 sh -c 'for i in 1 2 3; do (sleep 0.1 &); done; exec sleep 300'
docker exec z ps -o pid,ppid,stat,comm

PID   PPID  STAT COMMAND
    1     0 S    sleep
    8     1 Z    sleep
   10     1 Z    sleep
   12     1 Z    sleep

With --init, Docker starts its bundled tini as PID 1 (/sbin/docker-init). It runs your command as its child, forwards signals to it, and reaps every orphan:

$ docker run -d --init --name z2 alpine:3.20 sh -c '…same…'
    1     0 S    docker-init
    7     1 S    sleep              ← no Z rows

Zombies cost a process-table slot each. A long-running container that shells out (health scripts, image converters, headless browsers) can eventually hit the PID limit and fail to fork. --init is a runtime flag. Kubernetes has no equivalent, so when an image needs an init, bake one in:

RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tini && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/bin/tini", "--", "docker-entrypoint.sh"]

tini reaps orphans only. If a process that is still alive spawns children and never waits for them, those zombies stay its children, and no init can help. That is a bug in that program. (In the same test, a Python 3.12 PID 1 happened to leave no zombies, so whether a given runtime reaps is something to test, not assume.)

Rule Use --init, or bake tini into the image, whenever PID 1 is not a program written to be an init (any image that spawns subprocesses).

Why Orphans are re-parented to PID 1, and only PID 1 can reap them. tini both reaps and forwards signals.

Trap ps inside the container shows Z or <defunct> entries growing over days, and eventually fork: Resource temporarily unavailable. docker top <name> -o pid,ppid,stat,comm shows them without needing ps in the image.

Rung 6 Entrypoint scripts end with exec "$@"

A shell script as ENTRYPOINT is the standard way to do setup before the real process starts: check required settings, render a config file, wait for a dependency, fix permissions on a volume. The script must finish by replacing itself with the real command:

exec replaces the shell process with the command, so the server takes over PID 1 and receives signals. "$@" is the list of arguments the script received, which is CMD or whatever was passed to docker run, with each word kept intact by the quotes. The ${1#-} test is a convention from the official images: if the first argument starts with -, the user passed flags, so they are prepended with the default program.

$ docker run --rm pantry-manual:d02 --version
pantry: starting gunicorn (REDIS_HOST=redis)
gunicorn (version 26.2.0)
$ docker run --rm pantry-manual:d02 python -c "print('bypassed')"
bypassed
$ docker run --rm -e REDIS_HOST= pantry-manual:d02
/usr/local/bin/docker-entrypoint.sh: 6: REDIS_HOST: REDIS_HOST must be set

Without exec, the shell stays as the parent, signals stop at the shell, and you are back at rung 1. Without "$@", CMD and the run arguments are silently ignored. The spot-the-bug file does both.

Rule End every entrypoint script with exec "$@", start it with set -eu, and keep it short.

Why exec hands PID 1 to the real process. "$@" passes the arguments through unchanged. set -eu stops on the first failed command or unset variable instead of starting a half-configured server.

Trap The script works, but docker stop takes ten seconds. In /proc/*/cmdline, /bin/sh /usr/local/bin/start.sh sits between PID 1 and the server.

Rung 7 STOPSIGNAL and the stop timeout

docker stop sends the image's STOPSIGNAL (default SIGTERM), waits a timeout (default 10 s), then sends SIGKILL. A server that drains connections on SIGTERM needs that window to be longer than its drain:

$ docker stop d02-d1           →  11s exit=137 logs: draining
$ docker stop -t 30 d02-d2     →  16s exit=0   logs: draining drained

The timeout belongs to the runner: docker stop -t 30, docker run --stop-timeout 30, Compose stop_grace_period: 30s, or Kubernetes terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30 (default 30, K4). Inside the image, make the server's own drain timeout shorter than the smallest grace period it will get. gunicorn's --graceful-timeout defaults to 30 s, longer than Docker's 10 s, which is why the golden file sets 8. Some programs want a different signal. nginx drains on SIGQUIT, so its official image sets STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT.

Rule Set the server's drain timeout below the runner's stop timeout, and set STOPSIGNAL only when the program drains on something other than SIGTERM.

Why After the timeout, Docker sends SIGKILL, which cannot be caught, and in-flight work is lost.

Trap Deploys drop a handful of requests every time and the container's exit code is 137 even though the app handles SIGTERM. Its drain is simply longer than the grace period.

Decide

PID 1 is… Signals Orphans Do this
A server that handles SIGTERM (gunicorn, nginx, JVM, a Go service) handled reaped by the server for its own workers exec form, nothing else
A runtime with no SIGTERM handler (Flask dev server, a bare script) dropped maybe not fix the program, or STOPSIGNAL/--init
A program that spawns helpers (shells out, headless browser) depends not reaped --init or tini in the image
A shell script stops at the shell not reaped exec "$@" at the end
/bin/sh -c (shell form) stops at the shell not reaped rewrite in exec form

The golden file

Pantry with an entrypoint script, gunicorn as PID 1, and a drain that fits inside the default stop timeout. The script comes in through a second, named build context (--build-context manual=.), because the main context is the Pantry app directory and the script lives with this chapter's files.

docker build --build-context manual=. -t pantry-manual:d02 -f Dockerfile ../../pantry
docker run -d --name d02-web --network d02net -p 8002:8080 pantry-manual:d02
docker exec d02-web cat /proc/1/cmdline | tr '\0' ' '   # …/gunicorn --bind 0.0.0.0:8080 …
time docker stop d02-web                                 # 0s, exit 0

Review checklist

Spot the bug

It serves requests, and the pull request says "adds 4 workers".

This file has 4 problems.

Show answers
  1. ENTRYPOINT /usr/local/bin/start.sh is shell form. PID 1 is /bin/sh -c /usr/local/bin/start.sh --workers 4, and the CMD words became arguments to sh -c, which ignores them. Only 2 workers booted. Use ENTRYPOINT ["/usr/local/bin/start.sh"].
  2. start.sh runs gunicorn without exec, so a second shell (/bin/sh /usr/local/bin/start.sh) stays between PID 1 and gunicorn. SIGTERM never reached gunicorn: docker stop took 11 s and exited 137. End with exec gunicorn …, or better exec "$@".
  3. start.sh ignores "$@" and hard-codes its flags, so neither CMD nor docker run IMAGE --version can change anything (--version just started the server). Move the flags to CMD and end the script with exec "$@", as in the golden file.
  4. The HEALTHCHECK calls curl, which python:3.12-slim does not have. After about 100 seconds the container was unhealthy, with "curl: not found" in the health log (D1, rung 6).

Docker manual · 3 · 9 min readContext and Cache#

In the story: a step in the recipe; unchanged steps are not cooked again · Write the Recipe Down

A build has two inputs: the Dockerfile and the build context, which is the directory you hand to docker build. It produces a stack of layers. BuildKit keeps every layer it has made and reuses one whenever it can prove the result would be identical. That proof is the cache key, and almost every slow build, bloated image or leaked file comes down to not knowing what goes into it.

A layer's key is its parent's key plus what the instruction depends on. For RUN, that is the command text, the build arguments in scope, and the checksums of any files it mounts. For COPY, it is the checksums of the copied files. When a key changes, that layer and every layer after it are rebuilt. Everything in this chapter follows from that one rule.

The ladder

Rung 1 The build context is everything you send

docker build -f Dockerfile <dir> sends <dir> to the builder (minus what .dockerignore excludes) before reading a single instruction. COPY can only see what was sent. To see what you are sending, copy Pantry into a scratch directory next to a 200 MB database dump and a .env file, then build with a naive Dockerfile:

#5 transferring context: 209.77MB 3.9s done
$ docker run --rm pantry-manual:d03-naive sh -c 'cat /app/.env; du -sh /app'
API_TOKEN=sk-live-not-a-real-token
201M	/app

The token and the dump are inside the image now. Anyone who can pull the image can read them, and deleting them in a later layer does not remove them from the earlier one (rung 4). On a remote builder the 210 MB also crosses the network on every build.

Rule Choose the smallest directory that contains what the image needs as the context, and never let secrets, data or .git into it.

Why The whole context (minus ignores) is sent to the builder, and COPY . . copies everything that was sent into a layer that lives forever.

Trap The image is far larger than the app, or a credential scanner flags it. docker run --rm IMAGE ls -A /app shows dotfiles you never meant to ship, and the build log's transferring context: line shows the size before anything else happens.

Rung 2 .dockerignore, written as an allowlist

.dockerignore at the root of the context excludes paths from it. Write it as an allowlist: ignore everything, then let back in only what the Dockerfile reads. A new file in the repository then stays out of images until someone decides otherwise.

# Allowlist: ignore everything, then let back in only what the image needs.
*
!app.py
!requirements*.txt

#4 transferring context: 215B 0.0s done
$ docker run --rm pantry-manual:d03-allow ls -A /app
app.py  requirements-serve.txt  requirements.txt

The context went from 210 MB to 215 bytes. Two details matter:

  • Placement. BuildKit first looks for <Dockerfile name>.dockerignore next to the Dockerfile (naive.Dockerfile.dockerignore, Dockerfile.dockerignore), and only falls back to .dockerignore at the context root. One context can therefore serve several Dockerfiles with different ignore lists. This manual's chapters build from examples/pantry this way.
  • Syntax. Patterns are Go filepath.Match plus **, matched from the context root, and later lines win. ! re-includes. Comments start with #.

Rule Keep a .dockerignore (or <name>.dockerignore beside the Dockerfile) that starts with * and re-includes only the files the build needs.

Why An allowlist fails safe: new files, secrets and build output stay out by default. A denylist (.git, node_modules) forgets whatever nobody thought of.

Trap After you add the allowlist, the build fails with "/config.yaml": not found. That is the allowlist doing its job: a file the Dockerfile copies was not re-included. Add a !config.yaml line.

Rung 3 Order layers from least to most often changed

Every layer after a changed one is rebuilt. So the order of instructions decides what an everyday code edit costs. Copy the dependency manifest and install dependencies first, and copy the code last:

Measured after appending one comment line to app.py:

bad order (COPY . . before pip):   11.4s   pip install re-ran
good order (requirements first):    1.7s   pip install CACHED, only COPY app.py re-ran

The same principle applies to every ecosystem. Copy package.json and the lockfile, then npm ci, then COPY . .. Copy go.mod and go.sum, then go mod download, then the source. Copy pom.xml, then mvn dependency:go-offline.

Rule Copy dependency manifests and install dependencies before copying source code.

Why A COPY key includes the checksums of the files copied, so COPY . . changes on every edit and invalidates the expensive install that follows it.

Trap Every build reinstalls all dependencies even though only code changed. The plain build log (--progress=plain) shows no CACHED line for the install step.

Rung 4 What does and does not invalidate the cache

Three measured surprises:

1) touch app.py (content unchanged)          → COPY app.py  CACHED
2) --build-arg BUILD_NUMBER=1 → 2            → every RUN after the ARG line re-ran, including one that never uses it
3) RUN apt-get update, rebuilt days later    → CACHED (the package lists are as old as the first build)
  1. Content, not timestamps. BuildKit hashes file contents, so git checkout or touch does not bust the cache, and only real changes do.
  2. An ARG taints every RUN after it. A build argument in scope is part of every following RUN's environment, so changing its value changes their keys, used or not. A BUILD_NUMBER, GIT_SHA or DATE argument declared near the top reruns the entire build on every commit. Declare such arguments as late as possible, right before the one instruction that uses them, ideally a LABEL at the end.
  3. The cache does not know the outside world changed. RUN apt-get update has the same text tomorrow, so its cached layer, with yesterday's package lists, is reused. When you later add a package on a separate RUN apt-get install line, it installs against stale lists and can fail with 404s. Always run update and install in one RUN, and use --pull or --no-cache in CI when you want fresh inputs.
RUN apt-get update \
 && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends tini \
 && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*

Deleting files in a later layer never makes the image smaller. The earlier layer still contains them, and the later one only adds a whiteout marker. Cleanup must happen in the same RUN that created the mess, as above, or in a stage that is not shipped (D4).

Rule Declare volatile ARGs just before their only use, keep apt-get update and install in one RUN that also cleans up, and remember that the cache matches text, not the internet.

Why A RUN key is its parent, its command text and the arguments in scope. File checksums matter only for files the step copies or mounts.

Trap Builds are slow on CI and fast locally. CI passes --build-arg GIT_SHA=$SHA to a Dockerfile that declares ARG GIT_SHA on line 2, and --progress=plain shows every step after line 2 running again.

Rung 5 Cache mounts: keep the package cache between builds, not in the image

RUN --mount=type=cache,target=<dir> mounts a directory that BuildKit keeps between builds and never puts in a layer. Point it at the package manager's download cache:

#9 3.147   Using cached flask-3.1.0-py3-none-any.whl.metadata (2.7 kB)
#9 3.485   Using cached gunicorn-26.2.0-py3-none-any.whl.metadata (5.5 kB)
$ docker run --rm pantry-manual:d03-cm sh -c 'du -sh /root/.cache/pip 2>/dev/null || echo "no pip cache in the image"'
no pip cache in the image

What it saves depends on how big your dependencies are. Measured when one dependency was added:

Dependencies No cache mount Cache mount
Pantry's own (5 small pure-Python wheels) 12.7 s 12.7 s
Pantry + pandas + pyarrow (~100 MB of wheels) 96.4 s 60.3 s

The image built with the mount was also 11 MB smaller (589 MB against 600 MB), because no download cache ended up in the layer.

A cache mount speeds up the case that layer caching cannot: the dependency layer has to rebuild because a manifest changed. Then the manager reinstalls everything, and the mount turns most downloads into local reads. It also removes the need for --no-cache-dir, since the cache never reaches the image. Common targets: /root/.cache/pip (pip as root), /root/.npm, /go/pkg/mod plus /root/.cache/go-build, /root/.m2, /var/cache/apt (with sharing=locked and the docker-clean hook removed).

Cache mounts live in the builder. They are empty on a fresh CI runner unless the builder itself is persistent, or you export the cache (D6). They are shared by every build on that builder that uses the same id (the target path, by default).

Rule Mount the package manager's download cache with --mount=type=cache in every dependency-install RUN.

Why The mount persists across builds without becoming part of any layer, so rebuilds reuse downloads and images carry no cache.

Trap The cache mount "does nothing" in CI. Each job gets a fresh builder with an empty cache. docker buildx du on the runner shows no exec.cachemount entries, so persist the builder or export the cache to a registry.

Rung 6 Bind mounts: read files without copying them into a layer

RUN --mount=type=bind,source=<path>,target=<path> makes files from the context (or another stage) visible during one RUN, without a COPY layer:

RUN --mount=type=bind,source=requirements.txt,target=/tmp/req/requirements.txt \
    --mount=type=bind,source=requirements-serve.txt,target=/tmp/req/requirements-serve.txt \
    --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip \
    pip install -r /tmp/req/requirements-serve.txt

The checksums of the mounted files are part of the step's cache key, so the install still reruns exactly when the requirements change. Nothing mounted stays in the image: ls -A /tmp in the golden image is empty. Bind mounts are read-only by default, and writes with rw are thrown away after the step. Use them for manifests, for build scripts you do not want shipped, and for large inputs such as a source tree a compiler reads once.

Rule Use --mount=type=bind for files a RUN needs to read but the image does not need to contain.

Why A bind mount contributes its files' checksums to the cache key without creating a layer, so the image holds only the step's output.

Trap The step fails with Could not open requirements file: … No such file or directory: '/tmp/req/requirements.txt' for a file you can see in the context. Every path the command reads must be mounted, and -r requirements-serve.txt pulls in requirements.txt, which needed its own mount here.

Rung 7 See what the cache did

docker build --progress=plain -t img .                       # every step, CACHED markers, timings, RUN output
docker history --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}' img      # size each instruction added
docker build --no-cache -t img .                             # ignore the cache entirely
docker build --pull -t img .                                 # re-resolve FROM tags (new base patch releases)
docker build --no-cache-filter test -t img .                 # rebuild one stage only (D4)
docker buildx du                                             # what the build cache holds, and its size

docker history is the quickest bloat detector. It shows that the broken file's rm -rf /root/.cache/pip layer added 12.3 kB and the pip layer underneath still holds 23.2 MB. Read it top to bottom as "newest first".

docker history --format '{{.Size}}\t{{.CreatedBy}}' pantry-manual:d03

Rule Read --progress=plain output and docker history whenever a build is slower or an image is bigger than you expect.

Why They show, step by step, which keys missed and how many bytes each layer added, which is all the cache knows.

Trap Builds look fast locally because of cache, and the first CI build or a teammate's clone takes twenty minutes. Run docker build --no-cache occasionally to see the true cost.

Decide

Speed problem Fix
Every code edit reinstalls dependencies Reorder: manifests, install, then code (rung 3)
Every commit rebuilds everything A volatile ARG declared early; move it down (rung 4)
Adding one dependency redownloads all Cache mount (rung 5)
Large context upload Allowlist .dockerignore (rung 2)
Fresh CI builder every job Registry or GHA cache export (D6)
Big image docker history; cleanup in the same RUN; multi-stage (D4)

The golden file

Pantry built for fast, clean rebuilds: an allowlisted context, bind-mounted manifests, a pip cache mount, and code copied last with --link. It produces the same 205 MB image as D1, and rebuilds in under 3 seconds after a code edit.

docker build -t pantry-manual:d03 -f Dockerfile ../../pantry     # transferring context: 215B
docker run --rm -u 0 pantry-manual:d03 sh -c 'ls -A /root/.cache /tmp'   # no cache, no requirements files

Review checklist

Spot the bug

It builds. It is slow on CI and larger than it should be.

This file has 5 problems.

Show answers
  1. ARG GIT_SHA is declared on line 2, so every RUN after it depends on it. Built with a new SHA and no file changed, every step from apt-get update to rm re-ran. Declare it just before the LABEL that uses it.
  2. apt-get update and apt-get install are separate RUNs, so the update layer is cached with stale lists and the next added package can 404. The lists also stay in the image (21.6 MB). Use one RUN that updates, installs and removes /var/lib/apt/lists/*.
  3. COPY . . comes before pip install, so every code edit reinstalls all dependencies. Copy requirements*.txt first and the code after the install.
  4. pip install runs without a cache mount or --no-cache-dir, so its download cache goes into the layer (23.2 MB against 20.9 MB). Use --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.cache/pip.
  5. RUN rm -rf /root/.cache/pip in its own layer frees nothing: docker history shows it added 12.3 kB while the pip layer below still holds the cache. The image is 259 MB against the golden file's 205 MB. Clean up in the same RUN (or not at all, with a cache mount).

Docker manual · 4 · 9 min readMulti-Stage Builds#

In the story: build in one kitchen, serve from a clean one · Ship It

A multi-stage Dockerfile has more than one FROM. Each FROM starts a stage with its own filesystem, and later stages copy only what they need from earlier ones with COPY --from. Whatever you do not copy (compilers, headers, test tools, package caches, source code) stays behind and never ships. That one idea gives you small images, one Dockerfile for dev, test and production, and tests that run as part of the build.

The ladder

Rung 1 A builder stage and a runtime stage

The basic pattern: build in an image that has everything needed to build, then start again from a small image and copy in the result.

d04-single-stage   1.63GB     /usr/bin/gcc  /usr/bin/make  /usr/bin/git
d04-two-stage      209MB      no gcc, make or git

The single-stage image built on python:3.12 ships a compiler, make and git, plus the 1.4 GB of Debian it took to get them. The two-stage image ships the same app and the same virtualenv on python:3.12-slim. A virtualenv is a good unit to copy: one directory holding every dependency. It has one condition, though. Its interpreter symlink points to the builder's Python (/usr/local/bin/python), so the runtime must have the same Python at the same path and the same minor version (rung 6 and the spot-the-bug show what happens otherwise).

Rule Build in a stage that has the tools, and ship a final stage that starts from a small base and copies in only the build output.

Why Each stage is a separate filesystem. Layers of earlier stages are never part of the final image unless copied, so tools and caches used to build cost nothing at runtime.

Trap The "small" image is still huge. The final stage was written FROM builder instead of FROM python:3.12-slim, so it inherited every layer. docker history shows the builder's apt-get layers.

Rung 2 Named stages and --target: dev, test and prod from one file

Name stages with AS and build any of them with --target. A stage can start FROM an earlier one. The golden file has four stages: deps builds the virtualenv once, test adds pytest and runs the tests, dev runs Flask's reloading server, and prod is the clean runtime.

docker build --build-context manual=. -f Dockerfile ../../pantry                          # prod (the last stage)
docker build --build-context manual=. --target dev -t pantry-manual:d04-dev -f Dockerfile ../../pantry
docker run -d -p 8004:8080 -v "$PWD/../../pantry":/app pantry-manual:d04-dev                # edits reload

alive
alive and reloaded
 * Restarting with stat
 * Debugger is active!

The dev image is the same base, the same dependencies and the same paths as production. Only the server and the debug settings differ, so "works in dev" means something. The tests/ directory and requirements-test.txt arrive through a second named context (--build-context manual=.), so the app's own directory stays clean. Compose can pick a target too (build: { target: dev }, D9).

Rule Name every stage, and build dev and test variants as --targets of the production Dockerfile instead of keeping separate Dockerfiles.

Why Shared stages build once and are cached for every target, and one file cannot drift out of sync with itself.

Trap COPY --from=0 (by index) works until someone adds a stage above it. Then it copies from the wrong stage: inserting a stage at the top of the spot-the-bug file produced "/venv": not found. Always copy --from=<name>.

Rung 3 BuildKit builds only what the target needs

BuildKit works backwards from the target and builds only the stages it depends on. Independent stages run in parallel: two stages that each sleep 5 seconds built in 8.5 s total. The other side of that is that a stage nothing depends on is skipped, test stages included. With a deliberately failing test:

prod without a dependency on test:   no [test …] steps; "naming to …d04-skip done"; exit 0
