golden prod (COPY --from=test …):    FAILED tests/test_app.py::test_livez - AssertionError: assert b'alive\n' == b...

The image built happily with a failing test, because nothing asked for the test stage. Two fixes:

  1. Make the final stage depend on the test stage. The golden file copies a marker file the test stage creates only when the tests pass:
   RUN python -m pytest -q tests && touch /tmp/tests-passed
   …
   COPY --from=test /tmp/tests-passed /tmp/tests-passed
  1. Or run the test target explicitly in CI (docker build --target test .) before building prod.

--no-cache-filter test reruns only that stage (and anything after it) while keeping the cache for the rest, which is useful to rerun flaky tests without reinstalling dependencies.

Rule Make the shipped stage depend on the test stage (or build --target test in CI), never assume a stage runs because it is in the file.

Why BuildKit resolves the dependency graph from the target backwards, and stages outside that graph are not built at all.

Trap A broken commit produced a green build and a pushed image. The build log has no [test …] lines at all. Count them, or grep for the test runner's summary line.

Rung 4 COPY --from an image

--from also accepts any image reference, not just a stage name. Use it to take one file out of an image without inheriting the rest:

# A static busybox, only for the healthcheck: distroless has no shell, curl or wget.
COPY --from=busybox:1.37-musl /bin/busybox /busybox
HEALTHCHECK --interval=10s --timeout=2s --start-period=10s CMD ["/busybox", "wget", "-q", "-O", "/dev/null", "http://localhost:8080/livez"]

Up 14 seconds (healthy)

The same pattern installs tools that publish themselves as images (a static binary in a scratch image is a common distribution format), and copies the CA bundle or time-zone data out of a builder (rung 7). The file must work in the target. A static binary works anywhere. A dynamically linked one needs the same libc.

Rule Use COPY --from=<image>@<digest or tag> to take single, self-contained files from other images, pinned like any base image.

Why The source image is pulled into the build but contributes only the copied paths, and pinning keeps the build reproducible (D6).

Trap The copied binary fails with exec … no such file or directory although ls shows it. It is dynamically linked against a libc the target lacks (glibc binary into Alpine, or anything into scratch). Copy a static build, such as busybox's -musl variant, which is static.

Rung 5 Choose the base: slim, alpine, distroless, scratch

The same Pantry app on five bases:

Base Size Shell Package manager libc Notes
python:3.12 1.63 GB yes apt glibc builder only
python:3.12-slim 209 MB yes apt glibc the safe default
python:3.12-alpine 102 MB yes (ash) apk musl wheels may not exist
gcr.io/distroless/python3-debian13 107 MB no no glibc Python 3.13 fixed by the image
scratch (Go, static) 9 MB no no none static binaries only

Alpine's catch is musl. Python wheels and many prebuilt binaries target glibc. When a package has no musllinux wheel, pip builds it from source, which needs compilers, takes minutes, and often fails:

#5 4.909   Downloading pyarrow-18.1.0.tar.gz (1.1 MB)
#5 37.53   Building wheel for pyarrow (pyproject.toml): started
#5 38.70   error: subprocess-exited-with-error

For interpreted languages, -slim gets most of the size win with none of the surprises. Distroless is the next step when you want no shell and no package manager to exploit. Scratch is for static binaries.

FROM python:3.12-alpine

Rule Default to -slim. Choose distroless to remove the shell and package manager, scratch for static binaries, and Alpine only after checking that every dependency has a musl build.

Why Size matters less than what is inside. Fewer packages mean fewer CVEs and less for an attacker to use, while a libc mismatch turns into build failures or subtle runtime bugs.

Trap The Alpine build takes twenty minutes on CI and works on a laptop with a warm cache. The log shows Downloading <pkg>.tar.gz and Building wheel for <pkg> where the Debian build said .whl.

Rung 6 Distroless, done right

Distroless images contain a language runtime, CA certificates, /etc/passwd with a nonroot user (65532), and nothing else: no shell, no package manager, no coreutils. They have two consequences you must design for. The runtime version belongs to the image (distroless python3-debian13 is Python 3.13.5 at /usr/bin/python3, debian12 is 3.11.2). And anything that needs a shell (shell-form CMD, entrypoint scripts, docker exec … sh) is gone.

Copying a virtualenv from a different Python breaks in a confusing way:

exec /venv/bin/gunicorn: no such file or directory

The file exists. Its shebang points to /venv/bin/python, a symlink to /usr/local/bin/python3.12, which does not exist in this image. The fix is to build with the same Python minor version as the runtime, and install into a plain directory used with PYTHONPATH, so there are no symlinks to break:

Hello from Pantry (v1). You are visitor #1. Served by bd68d2bd6db3.
Up 14 seconds (healthy)
$ docker exec d04-dl sh
exec: "sh": executable file not found in $PATH
$ docker exec d04-dl /busybox id
uid=65532(nonroot) gid=65532(nonroot) groups=65532(nonroot)

The image's ENTRYPOINT is /usr/bin/python3.13, so CMD supplies only arguments (-m gunicorn …). To debug a shell-less container, temporarily run the :debug (or :debug-nonroot) variant of the same distroless image, which adds a busybox shell at /busybox/sh, or, in Kubernetes, attach an ephemeral debug container (K11).

Rule For distroless, build with the exact Python minor version of the runtime image, install into a directory on PYTHONPATH, use the :nonroot tag, and write CMD as arguments to the image's entrypoint.

Why Distroless fixes the interpreter's version and path, and has no shell to run scripts or shell-form commands.

Trap exec …: no such file or directory for a file that ls shows. The interpreter named in its shebang (or symlink) is missing. docker run --rm --entrypoint /busybox IMAGE ls -l /venv/bin/python (with busybox copied in) shows where the link points.

Rung 7 Static binaries on scratch

scratch is the empty image. A statically linked binary is all it needs, and Go makes one with CGO_ENABLED=0:

with certs:    upstream status: 200 OK
without certs: Get "https://www.docker.com/": tls: failed to verify certificate: x509: certificate signed by unknown authority
listening on :8080 as uid 65532

Everything a normal base gives you implicitly must be copied in explicitly:

  • CA certificates for outbound TLS, as above.
  • Time-zone data (/usr/share/zoneinfo, or Go's -tags timetzdata) if you call time.LoadLocation.
  • /etc/passwd only if something looks up a user name. A numeric USER 65532:65532 works without it.
  • A writable /tmp if the program needs one (mount a tmpfs, D5).

The result is 9 MB, and docker stop took about a second. The Go runtime exits on SIGTERM even as PID 1, unlike Python (D2).

Rule Ship static binaries on scratch (or distroless/static) and copy in CA certificates and anything else the binary reads from the filesystem.

Why scratch has no files at all, so every file the program opens at runtime must come from a COPY.

Trap Outbound HTTPS calls fail only in the container with x509: certificate signed by unknown authority. The image has no CA bundle.

Decide

You have… Build stage Runtime stage
Python, Node, Ruby service full or slim image + deps -slim of the same version, copy the venv / node_modules
Same, hardened slim of the runtime's exact minor version, install to a directory distroless/<lang>:nonroot
Go, Rust (static) golang, rust scratch or distroless/static:nonroot + CA certs
Java JDK image + Maven/Gradle JRE or distroless/java
Static website node to build nginx:alpine, or caddy
Needs a shell at runtime any -slim (distroless and scratch have none)

The golden file

Pantry as one file with four targets: deps, test, dev and prod. Tests must pass for prod to build, dev reloads on edits, and prod is a fresh slim base with only the virtualenv and the code. D5 hardens this exact file into the final golden Dockerfile.

docker build --build-context manual=. -t pantry-manual:d04 -f Dockerfile ../../pantry     # … 2 passed in 0.52s; 209MB
docker build --build-context manual=. --target dev -t pantry-manual:d04-dev -f Dockerfile ../../pantry

Review checklist

Spot the bug

It builds, the pull request description says "tests run in the build", and the image is small.

This file has 4 problems.

Show answers
  1. The builder is python:3.13 and the runtime python:3.12-slim. The venv holds lib/python3.13, so the container dies with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'gunicorn'. Build and run on the same version, and use the PYTHON_VERSION argument in both stages.
  2. Nothing depends on the test stage, so BuildKit skipped it. The build log has zero [test …] steps. Copy a marker from it into the final stage, or build --target test in CI.
  3. COPY --from=0 copies by index. With one stage added at the top it copied from the wrong stage and failed with "/venv": not found. Use --from=builder.
  4. APP_VERSION is declared before the first FROM and never redeclared, so the label is empty ('') despite --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.4.0 (D1, rung 2). Add ARG APP_VERSION inside the final stage.

Docker manual · 5 · 10 min readUsers and Permissions#

In the story: the cook who works the kitchen, and the keys they are given · Ship It, The Night It Fell Over

A container is a normal Linux process with a fence around it. Inside the fence it has a user ID, a group ID, a set of capabilities (slices of root's power) and a filesystem whose files have owners and modes. By default that user is root (UID 0), with a dozen capabilities, on a writable filesystem. That is the same UID 0 the host kernel trusts, kept in check only by the fence. If the fence has a hole (a kernel bug, a mounted Docker socket, a --privileged flag, a writable host path), root inside becomes root outside.

This chapter takes the process from "root on a writable filesystem" to "an unprivileged numeric user, no capabilities, no way to gain more, and a read-only filesystem except for the paths it needs". Each step is measured. The last step is the golden Dockerfile for Pantry.

Without user namespaces (rung 7), there is one UID space. UID 10001 in the container is UID 10001 on the host, which is why ownership of mounted files matters.

The ladder

Rung 1 Root is the default, and what that means

$ docker run --rm python:3.12-slim sh -c 'id; grep -E "^Cap(Eff|Bnd)" /proc/self/status'
uid=0(root) gid=0(root) groups=0(root)
CapEff:	00000000a80425fb
CapBnd:	00000000a80425fb

a80425fb is Docker's default capability set: CHOWN, DAC_OVERRIDE (ignore file permissions), FOWNER, FSETID, KILL, SETGID, SETUID, SETPCAP, NET_BIND_SERVICE, NET_RAW, SYS_CHROOT, MKNOD, AUDIT_WRITE and SETFCAP. Root in a container cannot load kernel modules or remount the host, but it can read and write any file it can see, change ownership, and create raw sockets. Every file a root process writes to a bind mount is root-owned on a Linux host.

The cure starts with one line:

USER 10001:10001

$ docker run --rm -u 10001 python:3.12-slim grep -E '^Cap(Eff|Bnd)' /proc/self/status
CapEff:	0000000000000000
CapBnd:	00000000a80425fb

A non-root user has no effective capabilities. The bounding set (CapBnd) is still there, and rung 5 deals with it.

Rule Every production image ends with a non-root USER.

Why Without user namespaces, UID 0 in the container is UID 0 on the host, so any escape, or any host path mounted in, is exposed to full root.

Trap docker image inspect -f 'User={{.Config.User}}' IMAGE prints User= (empty) or User=root, and nobody noticed because the app works the same.

Rung 2 Fixed numeric UID and GID, and why the number matters

USER app and USER 10001 both drop root. Only the second is verifiable without reading the image's /etc/passwd, and Kubernetes refuses to guess:

$ kubectl get pod d05-named d05-numeric          # both with securityContext.runAsNonRoot: true
NAME          READY   STATUS                       RESTARTS   AGE
d05-named     0/1     CreateContainerConfigError   0          8s
d05-numeric   1/1     Running                      0          8s
container has runAsNonRoot and image has non-numeric user (app), cannot verify user is non-root

Create the account with explicit numbers and use the numbers in USER:

RUN groupadd --system --gid 10001 pantry \
 && useradd --system --uid 10001 --gid pantry --no-create-home --home-dir /nonexistent \
            --shell /usr/sbin/nologin pantry
USER 10001:10001

Why create the account at all, if the number is enough? A UID with no /etc/passwd entry works, but tools notice:

$ docker run --rm -u 10001:10001 python:3.12-slim sh -c 'id; echo HOME=$HOME; whoami'
uid=10001 gid=10001 groups=10001
HOME=/
whoami: cannot find name for user ID 10001

Why 10001 and not whatever useradd picks? A bare useradd app takes the first free ID, which on Debian is 1000. That is also the first human user on most Linux hosts, so files the container writes to a bind mount become that person's files, and the number changes if a base-image update adds an account. Pick a high number nobody uses on hosts (10001 and 65532, distroless's nonroot, are common), and keep it identical in every image, Compose file and Kubernetes securityContext.

Rule Create the runtime user with an explicit UID and GID above 10000, and write USER <uid>:<gid> with numbers.

Why Numbers are what the kernel and Kubernetes check. A name must be resolved through the image's /etc/passwd, which runAsNonRoot will not trust.

Trap The pod sits in CreateContainerConfigError, and kubectl describe pod says image has non-numeric user (app), cannot verify user is non-root.

Rung 3 Who owns what: code read-only, one writable directory

The runtime user needs to read the code and dependencies and write almost nothing. So leave the code owned by root (COPY's default) and give the user exactly one writable directory:

COPY --from=deps /venv /venv
WORKDIR /app
COPY app.py .
RUN install -d -o 10001 -g 10001 -m 0750 /data
USER 10001:10001

$ docker run --rm -u 10001 pantry-manual:d05 sh -c 'echo x >> /app/app.py; touch /venv/bin/evil'
sh: 1: cannot create /app/app.py: Permission denied
touch: cannot touch '/venv/bin/evil': Permission denied

The common opposite, COPY --chown=app:app . /app plus chown -R app /venv "so permissions just work", hands an attacker who gets code execution in the process the ability to rewrite the application and plant files in its PATH. The spot-the-bug image allowed exactly that. When you genuinely need ownership on copied files (a writable cache directory, files a non-root process must replace), set it during the copy, never with a later RUN chown -R:

chown-run:   632MB    176MB venv layer + 172MB chown layer (every file copied again)
chown-copy:  407MB    172MB COPY --chown layer

A chown in a later layer rewrites the metadata of every file, and on overlay filesystems that copies every file into the new layer. COPY --chown and COPY --chmod set ownership and mode as the files are written, in one layer.

Rule Leave code and dependencies root-owned and not writable by the runtime user, create only the directories it must write with install -d -o <uid>, and use COPY --chown/--chmod instead of RUN chown/chmod on copied files.

Why A process that cannot write its own code cannot be made to modify it, and a recursive chown after a copy duplicates every file into a new layer.

Trap The image doubles in size after "fixing permissions". docker history shows a chown -R layer as large as the layer before it.

Rung 4 A read-only root filesystem, with tmpfs where needed

--read-only mounts the container's root filesystem read-only. Nothing can be added, changed or deleted anywhere except mounted volumes and tmpfs. That stops downloaded tools, modified binaries and web shells. Most programs need a scratch directory, though:

$ docker run --rm --read-only pantry-manual:d04
FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No usable temporary directory found in ['/tmp', '/var/tmp', '/usr/tmp', '/app']
$ docker run -d --read-only --tmpfs /tmp pantry-manual:d04 …
Hello from Pantry (v1). You are visitor #1.
touch: cannot touch '/app/x': Read-only file system
/tmp writable

gunicorn keeps worker heartbeat files in a temporary directory, so /tmp must be writable. A tmpfs is an in-memory filesystem that vanishes with the container. Find what a program writes by running it read-only and reading the errors, or by running it normally and checking docker diff <container>, which lists every path added (A) or changed (C) since start. For Pantry it lists nothing, because gunicorn's heartbeat files are created and immediately unlinked. Set PYTHONDONTWRITEBYTECODE=1 so Python does not try to write .pyc files next to the code. Persistent data goes on a volume (-v pantry-data:/data, D8).

docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp -v pantry-data:/data pantry-manual:d05
docker diff <container>          # what a normal run writes: candidates for tmpfs or a volume

Rule Run with --read-only, adding --tmpfs for scratch paths and volumes for data, and design the image so that works.

Why A read-only root filesystem makes every unexpected write fail loudly, which blocks most post-exploitation steps and documents exactly where state lives.

Trap The app works locally and crashes in production, where the platform enforces a read-only root (Kubernetes readOnlyRootFilesystem, K3), with "Read-only file system" or "No usable temporary directory". Run it read-only locally first.

Rung 5 Drop capabilities and forbid privilege escalation

Even as UID 10001, two doors remain open. The capability bounding set is still full, and setuid binaries can raise the effective user. A deliberately setuid copy of id shows the second door:

setuid binary, default:            uid=10001 gid=10001 euid=0(root) groups=10001
with --cap-drop ALL only:          uid=10001 gid=10001 euid=0(root) groups=10001
with no-new-privileges:            uid=10001 gid=10001 groups=10001

The user ran a setuid program and became root (euid=0). Dropping capabilities removed root's powers (chown as root then fails with "Operation not permitted"), but not its identity, and identity is enough to read and write root-owned files. Only no-new-privileges stopped the escalation itself. Use both:

docker run --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges pantry-manual:d05

CapEff:	0000000000000000
CapBnd:	0000000000000000
NoNewPrivs:	1

Add back only what the program needs, by name: --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE to bind ports below 1024 as non-root on hosts that require it. Docker itself sets net.ipv4.ip_unprivileged_port_start=0 inside containers, so binding port 80 as UID 10001 worked here without it, but Kubernetes nodes may not. Never use --privileged. It grants every capability and every device.

Rule Run every container with --cap-drop ALL and --security-opt no-new-privileges, adding single capabilities back only when a measured need exists.

Why Capabilities are root's powers, and setuid is a way to become root. Dropping one without blocking the other leaves a path open.

Trap A "non-root" container shows euid=0 in /proc/<pid>/status (Uid: line, second field) after running a helper binary. find / -xdev -perm -4000 -type f lists the setuid binaries that make it possible: python:3.12-slim ships eight (su, passwd, mount, umount, newgrp, chfn, chsh, gpasswd).

Rung 6 Bind mounts and the UID mismatch

Bind mounts share a host directory with the container, and on Linux they share UIDs too. Docker Desktop on macOS and Windows hides this: its file-sharing layer maps every file to your host user. That is convenient, and it means "works on my Mac" says nothing about Linux. A named volume keeps real Linux ownership, so it stands in for a Linux host directory owned by UID 1000:

$ ls -ldn /srv/project                       → drwxr-xr-x 1000 1000
$ docker run -u 10001:10001 -v …:/srv/project … touch /srv/project/out.txt
touch: cannot touch '/srv/project/out.txt': Permission denied
$ docker run -u 1000:1000 …                  → ok

A brand-new named volume mounted where the image has no directory is created root-owned, with the same result for a non-root user:

$ docker run --rm -u 10001:10001 -v d05-data:/data python:3.12-slim sh -c 'ls -ldn /data; touch /data/x'
drwxr-xr-x 2 0 0 4096 Oct 23 22:52 /data
touch: cannot touch '/data/x': Permission denied

Mounted over a directory the image does have, a new volume copies that directory's contents and ownership. That is why the golden file creates /data owned by 10001:

$ docker run --rm --read-only --tmpfs /tmp -v d05-golden-data:/data pantry-manual:d05 sh -c 'ls -ldn /data; touch /data/visits'
drwxr-x--- 2 10001 10001 4096 Oct 23 22:56 /data
/data writable

For development bind mounts on Linux, run as yourself: docker run --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD":/src …, or Compose user: "${UID}:${GID}".

docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" -v "$PWD":/src -w /src python:3.12-slim python -c 'open("out.txt","w")'

Rule Create every mount point in the image owned by the runtime UID, and for host bind mounts, run as the host user's UID or chown the host directory.

Why Ownership is a number, and the container's UID is checked against the host directory's numbers. Named volumes take their initial ownership from the image directory they are mounted over.

Trap CI on Linux fails with "Permission denied" writing to a mounted workspace that worked on every developer's Mac. Compare id in the container with ls -ln of the directory.

Rung 7 Rootless Docker and user namespaces

Everything so far limits what UID 0 can do. User namespaces change what UID 0 is. With userns-remap in the daemon ("userns-remap": "default" in daemon.json), container UIDs 0–65535 map to an unprivileged range on the host (such as 100000–165535). Root in the container is then nobody on the host. Rootless Docker goes further and runs the daemon itself as a normal user. Both are host settings, invisible to the Dockerfile, and they make the bind-mount ownership puzzle of rung 6 harder, because host and container numbers now differ by an offset. Kubernetes has user namespaces per Pod (hostUsers: false, K3).

docker info --format '{{json .SecurityOptions}}'    # shows "name=userns" or "name=rootless" when enabled

Rule Treat user namespaces and rootless mode as a second layer on hosts you control, and never as a reason to skip USER.

Why Remapping protects the host from container root, but the image must still be correct on hosts without it, which includes most CI runners and many clusters.

Trap After enabling userns-remap, existing named volumes show Permission denied. Their files are owned by the old, unmapped UIDs. ls -ln on the host shows the numbers, and the fix is to chown them to the remapped range.

Decide

Need Do Not
Run as non-root useradd --uid 10001 … + USER 10001:10001 USER app, or no USER
App must write somewhere install -d -o 10001 … + tmpfs or volume there chmod -R 777, chown -R app /app
Files owned by the user COPY --chown=10001:10001 RUN chown -R after copying
Port below 1024 listen on 8080 and map -p 80:8080 run as root
Debug as root once docker exec -u 0 <name> sh USER root in the image
Install a package USER root → RUN … → USER 10001 again ending the file with USER root
Container must manage the host it is an agent, not an app: review separately --privileged by default

The golden file

The golden Dockerfile for Pantry: D1's instructions, D2's PID 1, D3's cache, D4's stages and test gate, and this chapter's user, ownership, read-only layout and runtime flags. It passes the review checklist of every Docker manual chapter so far, and builds for linux/amd64 and linux/arm64.

docker build --build-context manual=. --build-arg APP_VERSION=1.0.0 --build-arg GIT_SHA=c16e39a \
  -t pantry-manual:d05 -f Dockerfile ../../pantry                                # 2 passed; 209MB
docker run -d --name d05-web --network d05net -p 8009:8080 \
  --read-only --tmpfs /tmp --cap-drop ALL --security-opt no-new-privileges pantry-manual:d05
docker exec d05-web sh -c 'id; grep -E "^(CapEff|CapBnd|NoNewPrivs)" /proc/1/status'
docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --build-context manual=. -t pantry-manual:d05-multi -f Dockerfile ../../pantry
# ~16 min on an Intel Mac: arm64 runs under emulation, tests included (D6 shows how to avoid that)

Review checklist

Spot the bug

It builds, the healthcheck passes, and "the container runs as app".

This file has 5 problems.

Show answers
  1. useradd --create-home app takes the first free UID, which was uid=1000(app): the first human user on most Linux hosts, and a number that can change. USER app is a name, so Kubernetes runAsNonRoot rejects it. Use --uid 10001 --gid 10001 and USER 10001:10001.
  2. The last USER root, added for the curl install, is never undone. The image config says User=root, and id in the container prints uid=0(root). Switch back with USER 10001:10001 after the install, or better, drop curl and use a Python healthcheck (D1).
  3. COPY --chown=app:app and chown -R app:app /venv hand the app its own code and dependencies. As app, the test wrote to /app/app.py and created /venv/bin/evil. Leave them root-owned.
  4. RUN chown -R app:app /venv in a separate layer copied the whole virtualenv again (24.8 MB on a 29.5 MB layer), giving a 277 MB image against the golden file's 209 MB. Use COPY --chown if ownership is really needed.
  5. chmod -R 777 /app makes every file world-writable and executable (-rwxrwxrwx), so any UID in the container can modify the code. Remove it: root-owned 0644 files are readable by everyone, which is all the app needs.

Docker manual · 6 · 10 min readSupply Chain and Secrets#

In the story: the cookbook library: which edition of the recipe you used, who wrote it, and what went into it · Ship It

Your image is built from other people's images and packages, by a build that may need credentials, for machines with different CPUs, and it is pulled by systems that have to trust it. Each of those is a place where something can silently change or leak:

  • a tag that points somewhere new;
  • a token that ends up in a layer;
  • an arm64 build that takes sixteen minutes;
  • a vulnerable library nobody looked at.

This chapter closes each gap with something you can check.

The ladder

Rung 1 Tags move; digests do not

A tag is a movable name. The registry can point python:3.12-slim at a new image whenever the publisher pushes, which for official images is every patch release and every Debian security update. While this chapter was being tested, the same tag resolved to two different images a few hours apart:

#4 [1/4] FROM docker.io/library/python:3.12-slim@sha256:78387bc3881b8273120a12ebe6c1ab22b018ccc2c9adf565ae1ac9b536e184ea
…later the same day…
#7 [deps 1/3] FROM docker.io/library/python:3.12-slim@sha256:a0f57064cbdcd6285fa45f51237ab0b35ea8ebaed06a1f5973e89e19dfb86704

A digest (@sha256:…) names content, and it can never point anywhere else. Pin the digest of the multi-platform index, not of one platform's manifest, so one reference works on every architecture. Keep the tag next to it for humans:

docker buildx imagetools inspect python:3.12-slim                 # "Digest:" line is the index digest

ARG PYTHON_IMAGE=python:3.12-slim@sha256:a0f57064cbdcd6285fa45f51237ab0b35ea8ebaed06a1f5973e89e19dfb86704
FROM ${PYTHON_IMAGE}

When a tag and a digest are both present, the digest wins and the tag is only a label. Pinning means updates are now your job. Let Renovate or Dependabot open a pull request when the tag's digest changes, so security fixes still arrive, through review and CI.

Rule Pin every FROM and COPY --from=<image> to tag@sha256:<index digest>, and automate the pull requests that move the pins.

Why A digest is the hash of the content, so a pinned build gets exactly the same bytes tomorrow, while a tag can be repointed at any time.

Trap A rebuild of an old commit behaves differently from the original build. Compare the FROM …@sha256 lines in the two build logs (--progress=plain): the tag resolved to a different digest.

Rung 2 Build secrets are mounted, never passed as ARG or ENV

A build that needs a token (a private package index, a private git repository, an API to download a licence) must not receive it as an ARG, an ENV or a file COPY. Build arguments are recorded in the image history:

WARN: SecretsUsedInArgOrEnv: Do not use ARG or ENV instructions for sensitive data (ARG "PIP_INDEX_TOKEN") (line 2)
$ docker history --no-trunc --format '{{.CreatedBy}}' pantry-manual:d06-arg | grep -o "PIP_INDEX_TOKEN=[^ ]*"
PIP_INDEX_TOKEN=tok-not-a-real-secret-123
occurrences in the saved ARG image: 1

Anyone who can pull the image can read the token. A secret mount makes the value available as a file (or an environment variable) for one RUN, and nowhere else:

export PIP_INDEX_TOKEN=…
docker build --secret id=pip_token,env=PIP_INDEX_TOKEN -f secret-mount.Dockerfile .

#7 0.221 token is 25 bytes
#8 [stage-0 3/3] RUN --mount=type=secret,id=pip_token,env=PIP_TOKEN,required=true     test -n "****" && …
occurrences of the token in history: 0
occurrences in the saved image tarball: 0

BuildKit even masked the value in the log (****). --secret takes the value from an environment variable (env=) or a file (src=). required=true fails the build with secret pip_token: not found when it is missing, instead of silently building without it. The secret is not part of the cache key, so rotating a token does not trigger a rebuild. If a step's output depends on the secret, add a cache-busting input on purpose.

Rule Pass build-time credentials only with --secret and RUN --mount=type=secret,…,required=true, never with ARG, ENV or COPY.

Why A secret mount exists only for the duration of one RUN and is never written to a layer, the history or the cache.

Trap The build prints SecretsUsedInArgOrEnv, or docker history --no-trunc IMAGE shows TOKEN=…. Rotate the credential first, then fix the Dockerfile: the image is already out there.

Rung 3 SSH forwarding for private repositories

For git clone or go mod download from private repositories over SSH, forward your agent instead of copying a key:

$ eval $(ssh-agent -s) && ssh-add ~/.ssh/id_ed25519
$ docker build --ssh default -f ssh-mount.Dockerfile .
#8 0.293 256 SHA256:FlO7JfR3Ohm1IlOohdH3+iaehEPAPd8SZ3zJndgqjfo d06-throwaway (ED25519)
$ # without --ssh:
ERROR: failed to solve: process "/bin/sh -c ssh-add -l" did not complete successfully: exit code: 2

The build can use the key through the agent socket, but the private key never enters the build. Combine it with known_hosts pinned in the image (RUN mkdir -p ~/.ssh && ssh-keyscan github.com >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts, or better, the host's published keys copied in) so the clone does not prompt or trust blindly.

Rule Use --ssh default with RUN --mount=type=ssh for SSH access during a build, and never COPY a private key, even into a stage you do not ship.

Why The agent signs on the build's behalf without revealing the key. A copied key sits in a layer of the builder stage, which is in the build cache and in any image built from that stage.

Trap Permission denied (publickey) inside the build although ssh -T git@github.com works on your machine. The RUN has no --mount=type=ssh, or docker build was called without --ssh default.

Rung 4 Multi-platform builds without emulation

docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 builds one image per platform and joins them in an index, so docker pull on a Mac with Apple silicon, on a Raspberry Pi and on an x86 server each gets the right one. By default each platform's RUN steps execute as that platform, under QEMU emulation when the CPU differs, which is slow:

golden Pantry Dockerfile (pip install + tests), linux/amd64 + linux/arm64 on an Intel Mac:  976 s

BuildKit gives every stage four automatic arguments: BUILDPLATFORM, BUILDARCH (the machine running the build), TARGETPLATFORM and TARGETARCH (the image being built). For compiled languages, run the build stage natively and cross-compile:

Measured for the two-platform Go image, built with --no-cache on an Intel Mac:

go/emulated.Dockerfile (build stage emulated for arm64):   414 s
go/Dockerfile (FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM, GOARCH):     40 s

The same arguments pick the right download for each target without emulation, even for tools that cannot cross-compile:

building on amd64, fetching the amd64 binary
running on x86_64
building on amd64, fetching the arm64 binary
running on aarch64

Interpreted languages with native wheels or modules (Python, Node) usually need either emulation for the install step, or a native builder for each architecture (docker buildx create --append with an arm64 node, or CI runners per architecture).

Rule Build every image you publish for each platform it runs on, running build stages --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM and cross-compiling with TARGETOS/TARGETARCH wherever the toolchain allows.

Why A single-platform image fails, or runs emulated and slowly, on other CPUs. Cross-compiling on the build platform avoids emulating every compiler instruction.

Trap The image works in CI and fails on an Apple-silicon laptop with exec format error or a warning that the requested image's platform (linux/amd64) does not match the detected host platform. docker buildx imagetools inspect IMAGE lists which platforms the tag really contains.

Rung 5 SBOMs and provenance attestations

BuildKit can attach two attestations to the image index: an SBOM (software bill of materials: every package in the image) and provenance (how, from what, and by which builder it was built, in SLSA format). Both travel with the image in the registry:

docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 --sbom=true --provenance=mode=max \
  -t localhost:5001/pantry-manual:d06-arch --push -f targetarch.Dockerfile .
docker buildx imagetools inspect localhost:5001/pantry-manual:d06-arch --format '{{json .SBOM}}'
docker buildx imagetools inspect localhost:5001/pantry-manual:d06-arch --format '{{json .Provenance}}'

Platform:    unknown/unknown
  vnd.docker.reference.type:   attestation-manifest
linux/amd64 15 packages, e.g. ['alpine-baselayout', 'alpine-baselayout-data', 'alpine-keys', 'apk-tools', 'busybox', 'busybox-binsh']
provenance keys: ['buildConfig', 'buildType', 'builder', 'invocation', 'materials', 'metadata']

When a new CVE is published, the SBOMs of your registry answer "which of our images contain this package, at which version?" without rebuilding anything. mode=max provenance records the full build definition, including build-argument names and values, which is one more reason secrets never go through ARG. Attestations need a registry (or an OCI output). The classic docker image store keeps only the image, so push or use the containerd image store.

Rule Publish every release image with --sbom=true --provenance=mode=max.

Why They record what is inside the image and how it was built, attached to the exact digest, so audits and vulnerability response work from facts instead of rebuilding to find out.

Trap imagetools inspect shows no attestation-manifest entries. The build loaded into the local image store instead of pushing, or the CI builder's driver does not support attestations. Check for exporting attestation manifest in the build log.

Rung 6 Scan, and gate on what you can fix

A scanner compares the image's packages with vulnerability databases. Trivy needs no account and can scan a saved image without access to the Docker socket. On the golden images:

docker save -o d05.tar pantry-manual:d05
docker run --rm -v "$PWD":/in:ro -v trivy-cache:/root/.cache aquasec/trivy:0.76.1 image --input /in/d05.tar --severity HIGH,CRITICAL
Image HIGH + CRITICAL with --ignore-unfixed
pantry-manual:d05 (python:3.12-slim, Debian 13.7) 44 0
pantry-manual:d04-distroless 26 0
Pantry's Python packages (both images) 0 0

Two things are visible. Every finding was in the Debian packages, and none in Pantry's Python dependencies. And not one of them had a fix available yet. A gate that fails on every HIGH would have blocked every release until Debian shipped patches, so teams learn to ignore it. Gate on what you can act on (--ignore-unfixed --exit-code 1 for CRITICAL), look at the rest on a schedule, and rebuild often so that fixed packages arrive through new base digests (rung 1). Fewer packages also means fewer findings to triage: distroless had 26 against slim's 44.

Rule Scan every release image in CI and fail on fixable vulnerabilities above an agreed severity, and track the unfixed ones instead of gating on them.

Why A gate that blocks on findings nobody can fix gets bypassed. A gate on fixable findings forces exactly the update that would remove them.

Trap The scan is green and the image is still months old. Scanners report on what is in the image now, against the database now, so an image that is never rebuilt never picks up its base's fixes. Rebuild on a schedule and pin digests through Renovate.

Rung 7 Share the build cache through the registry

A fresh CI runner has an empty BuildKit cache, so every job rebuilds everything (D3). Export the cache to the registry next to the image, and import it at the start of the next build, on any machine:

docker buildx build --cache-to type=registry,ref=localhost:5001/pantry-manual:buildcache,mode=max …
docker buildx create --name d06-fresh --driver docker-container --driver-opt network=host --bootstrap
docker buildx build --builder d06-fresh --cache-from type=registry,ref=localhost:5001/pantry-manual:buildcache …

importing cache manifest from localhost:5001/pantry-manual:buildcache
CACHED

A brand-new builder with an empty cache rebuilt nothing. mode=max exports the layers of every stage, including deps and test, not only the final one, and that is what makes a cold runner fast. Other backends work the same way: type=gha for GitHub Actions, type=local for a directory a CI system caches, type=s3. Keep the cache in its own tag (or repository) so it does not clutter image listings.

Rule In CI, --cache-from and --cache-to … mode=max to a registry (or the CI's native cache), keyed per branch with a fallback to the main branch.

Why BuildKit can import a remote cache manifest and reuse any layer whose key matches, which turns a cold runner into a warm one.

Trap CI exports the cache but every build is still cold. It used the default mode=min, which exports only the final stage's layers, while the expensive deps stage was not exported. Look for CACHED on the dependency step in the build log.

Decide

Need Mechanism Not
Reproducible base tag@sha256:<index digest> + Renovate :latest, floating :3
Token during build --secret + RUN --mount=type=secret ARG, ENV, COPY .netrc, rm later
Private git over SSH --ssh default + RUN --mount=type=ssh copying id_rsa into a stage
arm64 + amd64, compiled FROM --platform=$BUILDPLATFORM + TARGETARCH emulating the compiler
arm64 + amd64, interpreted native builder per arch, or accept emulation shipping amd64 only
What is inside --sbom=true rebuilding to find out
How it was built --provenance=mode=max a wiki page
Vulnerabilities scan in CI, gate on fixable CRITICAL gating on every finding
Cold CI runners --cache-to/--cache-from type=registry,mode=max --no-cache every time

The golden file

The release script CI runs for Pantry. It builds the D5 golden Dockerfile for two platforms with attestations and a registry cache, pushes, gates on fixable critical vulnerabilities, and prints the digest to deploy. Verified against a throwaway local registry (registry:2 on 127.0.0.1:5001).

docker run -d --name registry -p 127.0.0.1:5001:5000 registry:2     # a throwaway registry to try it against
./release.sh
#   #9 importing cache manifest from localhost:5001/pantry-manual:buildcache
#   #44 exporting cache to registry
#   - '0': Clean (no security findings detected)
#   released localhost:5001/pantry-manual@sha256:3fab95cb02e77fd6fa9a795b8f066a586726e61bd4213ebc79cfa2d66aa0fc00

With the cache warm, the whole two-platform release took 18 seconds. The first version of this script read the digest with an imagetools inspect --format template that does not exist, got a multi-line listing instead, and Trivy failed on it. Reading containerimage.digest from --metadata-file is the reliable way: the build itself reports what it pushed.

Review checklist

Spot the bug

It builds and runs. Security review flagged it.

This file has 5 problems.

Show answers
  1. FROM python:3-slim floats across minor versions: it resolved to Python 3.15.1, while the code was tested on 3.12. Pin python:3.12-slim@sha256:<index digest> (rung 1).
  2. ARG PIP_INDEX_TOKEN puts the token in the image history (4 lines of docker history --no-trunc), and the build warns SecretsUsedInArgOrEnv. Use --secret and RUN --mount=type=secret (rung 2).
  3. The token is written to pip.conf in one layer and "removed" in a later one. The saved image still has the file with token__:tok-not-a-real-secret-123 in layer bd3640154cdf. The later layer adds only a whiteout entry (.wh.pip.conf). Pass the index URL through a secret-mounted environment variable for the one RUN that needs it.
  4. ADD https://… has no --checksum, so the build ships whatever the server returns today (D1, rung 3). Add --checksum=sha256:….
  5. COPY --from=busybox:latest is unpinned: a different busybox can arrive on any build. Pin it like a base image, for example busybox:1.37-musl@sha256:….

Docker manual · 7 · 8 min readNetworks#

In the story: doors between kitchens, and a serving hatch to the street · Memory and Neighbours

Every container gets its own network namespace: its own interfaces, its own localhost, its own routing table and ports. Docker connects namespaces to networks. On a single host that is usually a virtual bridge with an embedded DNS server. To let the outside world in, it publishes chosen ports on the host. Almost every networking surprise is one of three things:

  • the wrong network, so names do not resolve;
  • the wrong idea of localhost;
  • a port published wider than you meant.

The ladder

Rung 1 The default bridge has no DNS; user-defined bridges do

Containers started without --network join the default network, bridge. It is a leftover from early Docker: containers on it can reach each other by IP, but not by name. Any network you create yourself gets an embedded DNS server at 127.0.0.11, which resolves container names and aliases:

default bridge, by name:      gaierror [Errno -2] Name or service not known
default bridge, by IP:        connected
$ docker network create d07net
on d07net: nameserver 127.0.0.11; d07-redis -> 172.24.0.2; connected by name

docker network create d07net
docker run -d --name d07-redis --network d07net redis:7-alpine
docker run --rm --network d07net python:3.12-slim python -c "import socket; print(socket.gethostbyname('d07-redis'))"

And localhost inside a container is that container. REDIS_HOST=localhost points the app at its own namespace, where nothing listens on 6379: ConnectionRefusedError: [Errno 111] Connection refused. Compose creates a user-defined network for every project, which is why service names "just work" there (D9).

Rule Put containers that talk to each other on a network you created, and address them by container name or alias, never by IP and never as localhost.

Why Only user-defined networks have the embedded DNS, IPs change on every restart, and localhost is per namespace.

Trap Name or service not known for a container you can see in docker ps. docker inspect -f '{{json .NetworkSettings.Networks}}' <name> shows it is on bridge, or on a different network from its caller.

Rung 2 Publishing: choose the interface

-p 8000:8080 publishes container port 8080 on host port 8000 on every interface of the host. On a laptop that is your Wi-Fi address. On a server it is the public one:

-p 8010:8080             8080/tcp -> 0.0.0.0:8010     localhost: 200   192.168.0.39: 200
-p 127.0.0.1:8013:8080   8080/tcp -> 127.0.0.1:8013   localhost: 200   192.168.0.39: (refused)

docker run -d -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8080 pantry-manual:d05     # only this machine can reach it
docker port <name>                                         # what is published, and where

On a Linux server there is a second surprise. Docker writes its own iptables rules for published ports, and they are evaluated before the rules of host firewalls such as ufw or firewalld. ufw deny 6379 does not close a port that Docker published. Docker's documentation ("Packet filtering and firewalls") says so explicitly. Docker Desktop has no ufw, so this cannot be shown here. On servers, bind to 127.0.0.1 or a private interface, or do not publish at all and let a reverse proxy on the same network reach the container.

Rule Publish with an explicit address (-p 127.0.0.1:host:container for local access) and publish only the ports that must be reached from outside Docker.

Why A bare -p binds 0.0.0.0 (and ::). On Linux, Docker's iptables rules for it bypass the host firewall.

Trap A database you started "for local testing" shows up in someone's internet-wide scan. docker ps shows 0.0.0.0:6379->6379/tcp in the PORTS column, and nc <your LAN IP> 6379 from another machine answers.

Rung 3 Containers reach each other without publishing

Publishing is for the host and beyond. Containers on the same network reach every port the other container listens on, published or not, EXPOSEd or not. Redis in the golden layout publishes nothing and is reached by name:

docker run -d --name pantry-redis --network pantry-back --network-alias redis redis:7-alpine
docker run -d --name pantry-web --network pantry-back -e REDIS_HOST=redis pantry-manual:d05     # → redis:6379, nothing published

The flip side is that a shared network is a flat trust zone. Every container on it can reach every port of every other. Split networks by who needs to talk to whom (rung 4). Compose's expose: key and the Dockerfile's EXPOSE are documentation only and change nothing about reachability.

Rule Publish only the entry point (web), and reach everything else (databases, caches, internal APIs) over a shared network by name.

Why Published ports cross the host boundary. Network membership is what controls container-to-container access, regardless of EXPOSE or expose.

Trap The database is published "so the app can reach it", and the app then connects through host.docker.internal:5432. It works, and it has also exposed the database on the host's interfaces. Put both on one network and remove the -p.

Rung 4 Internal networks and containers on two networks

docker network create --internal makes a bridge with no route to the outside: containers on it can talk to each other and to nothing else. Ports cannot even be published from it. A container can join several networks, so the web tier can sit on a normal network (for its published port and outbound calls) and on the internal one (to reach the data tier):

web on pantry-front only:            the pantry is closed, Redis at 'cache' is unreachable
docker network connect d07-backend d07-web
web on both:                         Hello from Pantry (1.0.0). You are visitor #1.
from the internal network → 1.1.1.1:443:   OSError: [Errno 101] Network is unreachable
-p 8015:6379 on an internal-only container: (nothing published)

docker network create --internal pantry-back
docker network connect pantry-back pantry-web        # add a second network to a running container
docker network disconnect pantry-back pantry-web

--network-alias redis gives a container an extra DNS name on one network. Several containers can share an alias, and DNS then returns all of them, which is a crude form of load balancing. The app is configured with the role (redis), not the container's name.

Rule Put data stores on an --internal network, attach only the containers that need them, and give them role aliases.

Why An internal network removes both inbound publishing and outbound egress, which is what limits the damage when one container is compromised.

Trap A container on an internal network cannot download anything (Network is unreachable), including at startup: package installs, licence checks, telemetry. Do those at build time, or give that container a second, non-internal network.

Rung 5 none, host, and reaching the host

--network none gives a container only a loopback interface, which suits batch jobs that read and write mounted files and must never talk to anything:

$ docker run --rm --network none alpine:3.20 ip addr
1: lo: <LOOPBACK,UP,LOWER_UP> … inet 127.0.0.1/8 scope host lo
(the tunnel devices exist but are DOWN)

--network host shares the host's network namespace: no isolation and no port mapping, so the process binds the host's ports directly. On Linux it removes NAT overhead for very high packet rates. On Docker Desktop "the host" is the Linux VM, so it means much less there. Avoid it unless you have measured a need.

To reach a service on the host from a container, use host.docker.internal. Docker Desktop resolves it out of the box (here 192.168.65.254). On Linux, add it explicitly, and the same flag works everywhere:

docker run --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway alpine:3.20 grep host.docker.internal /etc/hosts

Rule Use --network none for jobs that need no network, avoid --network host, and reach host services through host.docker.internal with --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway.

Why none is the strongest isolation available. host removes isolation entirely. host-gateway resolves to the host's address on the bridge on every platform.

Trap The app reaches the host's database on a Mac and fails on Linux CI with Name or service not known for host.docker.internal. Linux needs the --add-host (or Compose extra_hosts) line.

Rung 6 Debug from inside the container's network namespace

Hardened images have no ping, dig, ss or curl. You do not need them in the image. Start a toolbox container in the target's network namespace with --network container:<name>. It sees the same interfaces, the same localhost and the same DNS:

docker run --rm --network container:d07-web2 nicolaka/netshoot:v0.13 sh -c \
  'ss -lnt; dig +short d07-redis; nc -zv d07-redis 6379'

LISTEN 0      2048         0.0.0.0:8080       0.0.0.0:*
LISTEN 0      4096      127.0.0.11:35865      0.0.0.0:*
172.24.0.2
Connection to d07-redis (172.24.0.2) 6379 port [tcp/redis] succeeded!

The order of questions is always the same:

  1. Is the process listening, and on which address? ss -lnt shows 0.0.0.0 or 127.0.0.1.
  2. Does the name resolve? dig. An NXDOMAIN means wrong network or wrong name.
  3. Does the port connect? nc -zv.
  4. Only then, does the protocol work? curl, redis-cli.

A server listening on 127.0.0.1 inside its container is unreachable from every other container and through -p. Programs must bind 0.0.0.0 in containers.

Rule Debug networking from a toolbox container sharing the target's namespace, in the order listen → resolve → connect → protocol.

Why --network container: joins the target's exact network stack without adding tools to the image.

Trap -p 8000:8080 is published, and curl localhost:8000 fails with curl: (52) Empty reply from server. ss -lnt in the namespace shows the app listening on 127.0.0.1:8080, which is only reachable from inside the container. Bind 0.0.0.0.

Rung 7 Other drivers, in one paragraph each

docker network ls                                    # bridge, host, none, and your own
docker network inspect pantry-back -f '{{.Internal}} {{json .IPAM.Config}}'
  • macvlan / ipvlan: the container gets its own address on the physical LAN, as if it were a separate machine. Use it for software that must be reachable on the LAN without port mapping (legacy appliances, some network tools). It needs a NIC in promiscuous mode, and by design the host cannot talk to its own macvlan containers.
  • overlay: one network spanning several Docker hosts (Swarm). In Kubernetes the CNI plugin plays this role instead (K8).
  • Custom subnets: docker network create --subnet 10.99.0.0/24 … when the default 172.17+.0.0/16 ranges collide with a corporate VPN, which shows up as "the VPN breaks when Docker is running".

Rule Stay on user-defined bridges for single-host work, and reach for macvlan, overlay or a custom subnet only for the specific problem each solves.

Why Bridges give isolation, DNS and port publishing with no host configuration. The other drivers trade isolation for reachability.

Trap After docker compose up, part of the office network becomes unreachable. A Docker bridge took a subnet the VPN routes. docker network inspect shows the subnet. Set default-address-pools in daemon.json, or pick subnets explicitly.

Decide

Need Network Publish
Two containers talk user-defined bridge, by name nothing
Browser on this machine same -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8080
Public service on a server user-defined bridge + reverse proxy only the proxy's 80/443
Database, cache --internal network, alias never
Batch job, no network --network none n/a
Reach a host service host.docker.internal + --add-host …:host-gateway n/a
Container needs a LAN address macvlan n/a
Containers across hosts overlay (Swarm) or Kubernetes n/a

The golden file

Pantry's network layout with plain docker commands: a front network with outbound access, an internal back network for Redis, the web container on both, and the only published port bound to loopback. D9 expresses the same layout as a Compose file.

./up.sh && curl -s localhost:8000/          # Hello from Pantry (1.0.0). You are visitor #1. …
curl -s -m2 192.168.0.39:8000/ || echo "not reachable from the LAN"
docker exec pantry-redis wget -q -T 3 -O /dev/null http://1.1.1.1 || echo "redis: no route out"
./down.sh

Review checklist

Spot the bug

"Pantry on a dev server, two commands."

This file has 4 problems.

Show answers
  1. -p 6379:6379 publishes Redis on every interface. From the LAN address, PING got +PONG with no authentication. Do not publish it.
  2. REDIS_HOST=localhost points Pantry at its own container: "Redis at 'localhost' is unreachable". Use the Redis container's name or alias.
  3. Both containers are on the default bridge, where names do not resolve: even pantry-redis gives Name or service not known. Create a network, preferably an --internal one for Redis, and attach both.
  4. -p 8000:8080 publishes the app on every interface of a dev server. Bind 127.0.0.1:8000:8080 and reach it through an SSH tunnel or a reverse proxy.

Docker manual · 8 · 7 min readVolumes#

In the story: the pantry shelf that survives the dish being thrown away · Memory and Neighbours

A container's own filesystem is a thin writable layer on top of the image. It disappears when the container is removed, and it is slow for heavy writes. Anything that must outlive the container, or be shared with the host or another container, goes in a mount. Docker has three kinds, and they behave differently in exactly the places that cause data loss.

The ladder

Rung 1 Three kinds of mount, three lifetimes

docker run --name d08-c -v d08-named:/named -v "$PWD/bind":/bind --tmpfs /scratch alpine:3.20 \
  sh -c 'for d in /container /named /bind /scratch; do mkdir -p $d; echo hi > $d/f; done'
docker rm d08-c
docker run --rm -v d08-named:/named -v "$PWD/bind":/bind --tmpfs /scratch alpine:3.20 sh -c 'cat /named/f /bind/f'

/container  gone
/named      hi
/bind       hi
/scratch    gone
  • Named volume (-v name:/path): storage Docker manages (under /var/lib/docker/volumes on Linux, inside the VM on Desktop). It survives docker rm, needs no host path, and keeps real Linux ownership. Use it for databases and any app data.
  • Bind mount (-v /host/path:/path): a host directory, shared live. Use it for source code during development and for config files you edit on the host. On Docker Desktop it crosses the VM boundary, which is slower for heavy I/O and remaps ownership (D5, rung 6).
  • tmpfs (--tmpfs /path): memory, gone when the container stops. Use it for scratch space and for secrets the app writes at runtime, especially with --read-only (D5).

Rule Put persistent data in named volumes, development source in bind mounts and scratch in tmpfs, and nothing important in the container's writable layer.

Why Each kind has a different lifetime and owner: Docker, the host, or memory. Only named volumes are both persistent and independent of a host path.

Trap After docker compose down and up, or a redeploy, the data is gone. It was written to a path with no mount, inside the container's writable layer. docker inspect -f '{{json .Mounts}}' <name> shows which paths are mounted.

Rung 2 Copy-up happens once, and only for empty volumes

When an empty named volume is mounted over a directory that has content in the image, Docker copies that content (and its ownership) into the volume. It happens once. After that, the volume's content wins, whatever newer images contain:

new volume over /srv/assets, v1 image:   VERSION app.css   → v1
same volume, v2 image:                   VERSION app.css   → v1     (v2's files and new.js never appear)
empty bind mount over /srv/assets:       0 entries                  (bind mounts hide, never copy)
--mount …,volume-nocopy:                 0 entries

docker run --rm -v d08-assets:/srv/assets pantry-manual:d08-v1 cat /srv/assets/VERSION    # v1, copied up
docker run --rm -v d08-assets:/srv/assets pantry-manual:d08-v2 cat /srv/assets/VERSION    # still v1

That is the right behaviour for data: a database's files must not be replaced by an image's defaults. It is a disaster for anything that belongs to the image, such as code, static assets or default config. Mount volumes only on paths that hold data the image does not ship. Copy-up is also why the golden Dockerfile creates /data owned by 10001: a new volume there starts with the right owner (D5).

Rule Mount volumes only over data directories, never over paths whose content ships with the image (code, assets, bundled config).

Why Docker copies image content into a volume only while it is empty. Later images cannot update a non-empty volume.

Trap The new release is deployed, the container runs the new image, and users still see the old CSS or old behaviour. docker inspect shows a volume mounted over the app directory, which serves the first version forever.

Rung 3 Prefer --mount, and read-only where you can

-v is short and forgiving. Given a host path that does not exist, it creates an empty directory and mounts that. A typo silently becomes "no config":

-v ./confg:/etc/app          → container sees 0 files; an empty "confg" directory appears on the host
--mount type=bind,src=./confg,dst=/etc/app
                             → invalid mount config for type "bind": bind source path does not exist

--mount takes explicit key=value pairs (type, src, dst, readonly, volume-nocopy, tmpfs-size) and fails on a missing source. Mount anything the container only reads as read-only. A compromised process then cannot tamper with config or with shared data:

docker run --mount type=bind,src="$PWD/config",dst=/etc/pantry,readonly pantry-manual:d05
docker run -v pantry-manual-data:/data:ro alpine:3.20 ls /data                    # short form, read-only

sh: can't create /data/f: Read-only file system

Rule Write mounts with --mount in scripts and docs, and add readonly (:ro) to every mount the container does not need to write.

Why --mount turns a missing source into an error instead of an empty directory, and read-only mounts make writes fail loudly.

Trap A container starts with default settings even though you mounted a config directory. ls on the host shows a new, empty directory next to the real one (confg/ beside config/), created by -v.

Rung 4 Back up and restore through a throwaway container

You never need to know where Docker keeps a volume on disk. To back it up, mount it read-only into a small container next to a host directory, and write a tarball:

The restore mirrors it, and refuses to overwrite a non-empty volume unless told to:

$ docker exec d08-redis redis-cli SAVE
OK
$ ./backup.sh pantry-manual-data ./backups
./backups/pantry-manual-data-20261023T233219Z.tar.gz
$ docker volume rm pantry-manual-data && ./restore.sh pantry-manual-data ./backups/pantry-manual-data-…tar.gz
restored … into pantry-manual-data
visits after restore: 5

--numeric-owner keeps the files' UIDs (Redis's 999 here), so the restored data is readable by the same user. Consistency is the application's business: tar copies files, not transactions. Flush first (redis-cli SAVE, pg_dump instead of copying PostgreSQL's files), or stop the writer for the duration.

Rule Back up volumes with a throwaway container that mounts the volume read-only, after making the application flush or pause, and test restores on a schedule.

Why The container sees the volume as plain files wherever Docker stores them. A backup that has never been restored is a guess.

Trap The backup file is never on the host. The tar wrote into the throwaway container's own filesystem, which --rm deleted, because no host directory was mounted as the destination. Check that the file exists after every run.

Rung 5 Anonymous volumes and how they leak

A volume without a name is anonymous. You get one from -v /path with no name, and from any image that declares VOLUME when you do not mount that path yourself. The official Redis image declares VOLUME /data:

$ docker image inspect -f '{{json .Config.Volumes}}' redis:7-alpine
{"/data":{}}
$ docker run -d --name d08-anon redis:7-alpine
volume ed73e237d52ca4f2… -> /data
$ docker rm -f d08-anon
ed73e237d52ca4f2… still exists

The data is not lost, but nothing will ever mount that volume again. The next docker run gets a new, empty one. The machine these examples ran on had 121 such orphans. Clean up deliberately:

docker rm -v <container>                   # remove a container and its anonymous volumes
docker run --rm …                          # --rm also removes the anonymous volumes
docker volume ls -f dangling=true          # volumes no container references
docker volume prune                        # removes unused *anonymous* volumes; -a includes named ones

Rule Name every volume you care about, run throwaway containers with --rm, and remove anonymous volumes with rm -v or volume prune.

Why Anonymous volumes outlive their containers but have no name to find them by, so data in them is effectively lost and disk usage only grows.

Trap After recreating a database container, the app starts with an empty database, and the old data is in a hash-named volume. docker volume ls -f dangling=true and docker run --rm -v <hash>:/d alpine ls /d find it. Copy it into a named volume.

Rung 6 tmpfs options, drivers and disk accounting

A tmpfs defaults to half of the machine's memory (3.9 GB in this VM), and it counts against the container's memory limit. Size it and set its mode:

docker run --tmpfs /tmp:size=64m,mode=1777 alpine:3.20 df -h /tmp
docker run --mount type=tmpfs,dst=/tmp,tmpfs-size=67108864 alpine:3.20 df -h /tmp
docker system df -v                     # space per image, container, volume and build cache

tmpfs                    64.0M         0     64.0M   0% /tmp
dd … stopped at 67108864 bytes (64.0MB)

Volume drivers put a named volume somewhere other than local disk. The built-in local driver can mount NFS or CIFS (syntax: docker volume create --driver local --opt type=nfs --opt o=addr=<server>,rw --opt device=:/export pantry-nfs; not run here, it needs an NFS server), and plugins target cloud block storage. Network storage behaves very differently under databases: latency, locking, fsync. Single-host Docker rarely needs it. Kubernetes' PersistentVolumes and StorageClasses are the standard answer at that scale (K7).

Rule Give every tmpfs a size, and check docker system df -v before blaming anything else for a full disk.

Why An unsized tmpfs can take half the host's memory, and volumes and build cache are the usual hidden consumers of disk.

Trap Processes in a memory-limited container die with Killed under load though their own memory looks small. They filled an unsized tmpfs, which counts against the limit: with --memory 64m, writing 200 MB to /tmp got dd killed and docker inspect reported OOMKilled=true. Size the tmpfs below the limit.

Decide

Data Mount Options
Database files, uploads named volume owner set by the image's directory (copy-up)
Source code in development bind mount :ro if the container must not write; --user $(id -u) on Linux
Config edited on the host bind mount, single file or directory readonly
Scratch, caches, PID files tmpfs size=…
Secrets at runtime tmpfs (or a secret mount in Compose, D10) mode=0700
Code, assets, bundled defaults none: they belong in the image
Shared between hosts Kubernetes PV, or NFS via the local driver test fsync and locking

The golden file

Backup and restore for any named volume. Run against Pantry's Redis volume, it round-trips the visit count and keeps owners intact.

docker exec pantry-redis redis-cli SAVE
./backup.sh pantry-manual-data ./backups
FORCE=1 ./restore.sh pantry-manual-data ./backups/pantry-manual-data-<timestamp>.tar.gz

Review checklist

Spot the bug

"Pantry with a nightly backup."

This file has 3 problems.

Show answers
  1. Redis has no -v, so its data goes into an anonymous volume created by the image's VOLUME /data. After docker rm -f pantry-redis and the same docker run, Pantry said "You are visitor #1", and the old count was stranded in a hash-named volume. Add -v pantry-data:/data.
  2. -v pantry-code:/app puts a named volume over the code directory. Copy-up filled it once, and after upgrading to an image whose app.py was changed, the container still served the old text. Remove the mount: code belongs in the image.
  3. The backup writes /backup.tar.gz into the throwaway container's own filesystem, and --rm deletes it. No backup file existed anywhere afterwards. Mount a host directory as the destination, flush Redis first (redis-cli SAVE), and read the volume read-only, as backup.sh does.

Docker manual · 9 · 9 min readCompose: The File#

In the story: a dinner menu that cooks several dishes together · The Whole Band

A Compose file describes a project: services (containers built or pulled from one definition), the networks they share, and the volumes they keep. docker compose up turns that description into containers, and running it again changes only what differs. Everything earlier chapters did with docker run flags (ports, mounts, users, capabilities, health checks) has a key here. What Compose adds is relationships: who starts after whom, what counts as ready, and which values come from outside the file.

The golden file for this chapter is Pantry: a built web service, Redis with a health check and a named volume, and a one-shot seed job that must succeed before the web service starts.

The ladder

Rung 1 Services: build, image, and the project

A service either builds an image from a Dockerfile or runs an existing image. With both keys, Compose builds and tags the result with the given name, instead of the generated <project>-<service>:

services:
  web:
    build:
      context: ../../pantry                 # the app's own directory
      dockerfile: ../manual/d05/Dockerfile  # the golden Dockerfile (path relative to the context)
      additional_contexts:
        manual: ../d05                      # what --build-context manual=… did on the command line
    image: pantry-manual:d09
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine

The project is the unit Compose manages. Its name comes from the top-level name: key (here pantry-manual-d09), from -p, or from the directory's name. Containers (pantry-manual-d09-web-1), the default network (pantry-manual-d09_default) and volumes (pantry-manual-d09_redis-data) are all prefixed with it, so two copies of the same file in different directories do not collide. Set name: explicitly so the project does not change identity when someone renames a folder.

Rule Give every Compose file a top-level name:, and give built services both build: and an image: name.

Why The project name prefixes every container, network and volume. An explicit name keeps them stable, and a named image can be pushed or reused by other services.

Trap After a colleague clones the repository into a differently named directory, docker compose up starts with an empty database. The project name came from the directory, so the volume name changed (foo_redis-data became bar_redis-data). docker volume ls shows both.

Rung 2 Ports, and the reachability you get for free

Every project gets its own network, and services reach each other by service name on any port. Publish only what the host needs, on loopback, with the port configurable:

    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:${WEB_PORT:-8000}:8080"  # loopback only; the host port is configurable

redis     running   Up 13 seconds (healthy)   6379/tcp
web       running   Up 6 seconds (healthy)    127.0.0.1:8000->8080/tcp

Redis shows 6379/tcp with no host side: the port exists on the project network and nowhere else. expose: exists, but like the Dockerfile's EXPOSE it only documents (D7, rung 3). Quote port mappings: unquoted 60:60 style values were once parsed by YAML 1.1 as base-60 numbers, and quoting avoids the whole class of problem.

Rule Publish only entry points, always as quoted strings with 127.0.0.1: for local work, and let services reach each other by service name.

Why Compose's project network already connects every service. ports: is only for traffic from outside Docker, and a bare host port binds every interface.

Trap docker compose ps shows 0.0.0.0:6379->6379/tcp for a database. Anyone who can reach the machine can reach the database (the spot-the-bug file answered PONG from the LAN).

Rung 3 environment, env_file and .env are three different things

These three are confused more than anything else in Compose:

  • environment: sets variables in the container.
  • env_file: loads variables from a file into the container.
  • .env (next to the Compose file) feeds interpolation of the Compose file itself, the ${VAR} expressions, and nothing else.
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: redis                     # the service name is a DNS name on the project network
      GREETING: ${GREETING:-Hello from Pantry}

Measured:

.env: GREETING=Hello from .env              → "Hello from .env (dev)…"
.env: UNUSED_SECRET=…  (not referenced)     → absent in the container
shell GREETING=… and .env                   → "Hello from the shell (dev)…"   (shell wins)
neither                                     → "Hello from Pantry" (the :- default)
env_file BOTH=from-env_file, environment BOTH=from-environment → BOTH=from-environment

Interpolation order, highest first: the shell's environment, then --env-file/.env, then the default written in the file. Inside the container, environment: wins over env_file:. The operators:

Expression Unset or empty Use
${VAR} empty string (with a warning) rarely
${VAR:-default} default optional settings
${VAR:?message} error, Compose refuses to run required settings and secrets
$$ a literal $ shell commands in command: 
error while interpolating services.web.environment.DB_PASSWORD: required variable DB_PASSWORD is missing a value: set DB_PASSWORD in .env or the shell

Rule Put container settings in environment: with ${VAR:-default} or ${VAR:?message}, keep .env for interpolation values (and out of git when it holds secrets), and remember that .env does not reach the container by itself.

Why Compose resolves ${…} before creating anything, from the shell first and .env second, while the container only ever sees environment: and env_file:.

Trap A variable in .env is "ignored" by the app. It is never passed to the container unless environment: references it (FOO: ${FOO}) or an env_file: lists the file. docker compose config shows the final environment.

Rung 4 Named volumes and networks belong to the project

Top-level volumes: and networks: declare resources that services mount or join by name, created with the project prefix:

  redis:
    volumes:
      - redis-data:/data                    # named: survives "down", unlike the image's anonymous VOLUME
volumes:
  redis-data:

pantry-manual-d09_redis-data
$ docker compose down        → containers and network removed, volume kept
$ docker compose down -v     → named volumes declared in the file removed too

Leave out the named volume and Redis's image-declared VOLUME /data still creates an anonymous one. It survives docker compose up re-creations, but down followed by up gets a new, empty one: the spot-the-bug project went from a counter of 1 to 0. To use a volume or network that exists outside the project (shared, or created by an operator), mark it external: true with its real name:, and Compose will neither create nor delete it.

volumes:
  shared-uploads:
    external: true
    name: uploads-prod

Rule Declare every persistent path as a named volume under top-level volumes:, and treat down -v as "delete the data".

Why Named project volumes are created once and reused across up/down cycles. Anonymous volumes are tied to one container's lifetime in practice.

Trap docker compose down && docker compose up -d and the database is empty. docker inspect -f '{{json .Mounts}}' <container> shows a 64-character anonymous volume name instead of <project>_<name>.

Rung 5 Health checks and depends_on conditions

depends_on: [redis] only orders container starts. It does not wait for Redis to be ready. With a database that takes a few seconds to start, the one-shot seed job ran too early:

seed-1  | Could not connect to Redis at redis:6379: Connection refused

Give the dependency a healthcheck, and depend on its health:

  redis:
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 2s
      timeout: 2s
      retries: 15
      start_period: 5s
  seed:
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy
    restart: "no"
  web:
    depends_on:
      redis:
        condition: service_healthy          # not just "started": answering PING
      seed:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

The three conditions are service_started (the default), service_healthy (needs a healthcheck) and service_completed_successfully (for jobs: migrations, seeding, cache warm-up). docker compose up -d --wait blocks until every service is running and healthy (or a job has exited 0), and returns non-zero if not. Use it in scripts and CI instead of sleep.

 Container pantry-manual-d09-redis-1  Healthy
 Container pantry-manual-d09-seed-1  Exited
 Container pantry-manual-d09-web-1  Healthy

Startup ordering is not a substitute for retries. Dependencies restart independently later, so the app must still survive a database that goes away for a while.

Rule Give every dependency a healthcheck, depend on service_healthy (or service_completed_successfully for jobs), and start with up --wait.

Why "Started" means the process exists, not that it accepts connections. The healthcheck is the only readiness signal Compose has.

Trap The stack works on a fast laptop and fails on CI with "connection refused" in the first seconds. depends_on was a plain list, so the app raced the database's startup.

Rung 6 Restart policies

restart: tells Docker what to do when the container's main process exits. Measured with a process that exits after one second:

restart: exit 3 (crash) exit 0 (finished) after docker stop/kill
"no" (default) stays exited (0 restarts) stays exited stays stopped
on-failure:2 restarted twice, then gives up stays exited stays stopped
unless-stopped restarted forever (7 in 20 s) restarted forever stays stopped, also after a daemon restart
always restarted forever restarted forever stays stopped until the daemon restarts

Services use unless-stopped. One-shot jobs must use "no" (or on-failure): the spot-the-bug file gave its seed job restart: always, and it ran 8 times in 15 seconds and never stopped. Three details:

  • Docker does not restart a container for being unhealthy. Only Swarm and Kubernetes act on health.
  • /crash killed one gunicorn worker, the master respawned it, and the container never restarted. Supervision inside the container hides crashes from Docker.
  • A manual docker kill or docker stop is never undone by unless-stopped.
    restart: unless-stopped

Rule Use restart: unless-stopped for long-running services and restart: "no" for jobs.

Why Restart policies react only to the main process exiting, and always/unless-stopped treat a successful exit like a crash.

Trap docker compose ps shows a job in Restarting (0) forever. Exit code 0 plus restart: always loops, re-running the job (and its side effects) every few seconds.

Rung 7 Overriding the command, running one-offs, and exec

command: replaces the image's CMD, and entrypoint: replaces its ENTRYPOINT (and, as with --entrypoint, clears CMD, D2). Write both in exec form (lists). In list form, $ must be doubled ($$HOME) when you mean the container's variable rather than Compose interpolation.

  seed:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: ["redis-cli", "-h", "redis", "SET", "visits", "${SEED_VISITS:-0}", "NX"]

Two commands cover day-to-day use:

docker compose run --rm --no-deps web python -c "print('one-off in a fresh web container')"   # new container, same config
docker compose exec web id                                                                     # inside the running one

run starts a new container from the service's definition (same image, environment, volumes and networks). --rm removes it afterwards, --no-deps skips starting dependencies, and --service-ports is needed if you want its ports: published. exec enters the existing container.

Rule Override with command:/entrypoint: in list form, run one-off tasks with compose run --rm, and inspect running services with compose exec.

Why run reuses the service's full configuration without touching the running container, and list form avoids shell parsing and signal problems.

Trap docker compose run web leaves a growing list of pantry-manual-d09-web-run-… containers in docker ps -a. Add --rm.

Rung 8 docker compose config is the truth

Compose merges files, applies defaults, resolves ${…}, converts short syntax to long, and warns about obsolete keys before it does anything. docker compose config prints the result. Every "why is it using that value" question starts there:

docker compose config                       # the fully resolved project
docker compose config --quiet               # validate only: exit code and errors
docker compose config --services            # list service names

WARN … the attribute `version` is obsolete, it will be ignored, please remove it to avoid potential confusion

The top-level version: key is from the Compose v1 file formats and Compose v2 ignores it, so delete it. Run docker compose config --quiet in CI. It catches YAML errors, unknown keys, and required variables that are unset.

Rule Validate every Compose file with docker compose config --quiet in CI, and read docker compose config when a value surprises you.

Why It shows exactly what Compose will act on after interpolation and merging, which is often not what the file appears to say.

Trap A setting "has no effect". docker compose config shows it under the wrong service or misspelled, or replaced by an override file (D10).

Decide

You want Compose
Wait for a database healthcheck + depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }
Migrations before the app job service, restart: "no", condition: service_completed_successfully
A required secret value ${VAR:?message} (better: secrets:, D10)
An optional setting ${VAR:-default}
Settings for the container environment: (or env_file:)
Values for the file itself .env / shell variables
