Data that survives down top-level named volume
A resource managed elsewhere external: true + name:
A one-off task docker compose run --rm <service> <cmd>
Scripted startup docker compose up -d --wait

The golden file

Pantry as one Compose file: the golden Dockerfile built through additional_contexts, loopback-only publishing with a configurable port, interpolated settings with defaults, health-gated startup with a seed job, the D5 runtime hardening as Compose keys, and a named volume.

docker compose config --quiet && docker compose up -d --wait     # redis Healthy → seed Exited → web Healthy
curl -s localhost:8000/                                          # Hello from Pantry (dev). You are visitor #1. …
docker compose down                                              # keeps pantry-manual-d09_redis-data

Review checklist

Spot the bug

"Pantry with a seed job." It comes up, and the web page loads.

This file has 6 problems.

Show answers
  1. version: "3.8" is obsolete. Compose warns "the attribute version is obsolete, it will be ignored". Delete it, and add name:.
  2. REDIS_HOST=localhost makes web talk to itself: "Redis at 'localhost' is unreachable". Use redis.
  3. depends_on lists only order starts. The seed job ran before Redis accepted connections ("Could not connect to Redis at redis:6379: Connection refused"). Add a Redis healthcheck and use condition: service_healthy (and service_completed_successfully for web on seed).
  4. restart: always on a one-shot job restarts it after every successful exit: 8 restarts in 15 seconds, state Restarting (0). Use restart: "no".
  5. ports: "6379:6379" publishes Redis on every interface (PONG from the LAN address), and "8000:8080" does the same for web. Remove Redis's ports: and bind web to 127.0.0.1.
  6. Redis has no named volume, so its data lives in the anonymous volume from the image's VOLUME /data. After down and up, the visit count was back to 0 in a new anonymous volume. Add redis-data:/data with a top-level volumes: entry.

Docker manual · 10 · 10 min readCompose: The Project#

In the story: the same dinner menu, cooked for a weeknight and for a wedding · The Whole Band

D9 wrote one file for one environment. Real projects have several environments (a laptop with live reload, CI, a staging host, production), optional tools, secrets that must stay out of git, and parts owned by different teams. Compose handles all of it with a few mechanisms:

  • several files merged in order;
  • profiles;
  • include;
  • extension fields;
  • secrets;
  • develop.watch.

Each mechanism has one rule that surprises people. This chapter measures all of them.

The ladder

Rung 1 One project per environment, by name

A project is identified by its name, and Compose owns every container, network and volume carrying that name, wherever the file that created them lives. D9 said to set name:. The other half of that rule is that two running copies (prod and staging on one host, two feature branches on one laptop) need different names. Otherwise the second up adopts the first copy's resources:

staging checkout (same "name: pantry", port 8100):  docker compose up -d
 Container pantry-redis-1  Running
 Container pantry-web  Recreate
prod :8000 → (gone)      staging :8100 → visitor #4      ← prod's Redis and prod's data

docker compose -p pantry-staging up -d             # or COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME=pantry-staging in that host's environment
docker compose ls                                  # every project on this Docker host, with its files

The file's name: is the default, and -p or COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME overrides it per deployment.

Rule Set name: in the file for the normal case, and give every additional copy on the same Docker host its own -p/COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME.

Why Compose matches existing resources by project-name labels, not by directory or file, so two copies with one name are one project.

Trap Deploying staging takes production down. docker compose ls shows one project whose CONFIG FILES column points at the staging checkout.

Rung 2 Override files and the merge rules

docker compose up with no -f reads compose.yaml and then, if present, compose.override.yaml, merging the second over the first. You can pass any list with -f a.yaml -f b.yaml. Later files win, but "win" means different things for different keys. Measured with docker compose config:

Key kind Example Merge
Scalars image, command, entrypoint, user, read_only replaced
Mappings environment, labels, deploy merged per key, later wins
Lists of strings ports, cap_drop, dns, expose appended
Mounts volumes, secrets merged by target path, later replaces the whole entry
Explicit ports: !override [...] replaced
Explicit build: !reset null, depends_on: !reset [] removed 
ports:   ['127.0.0.1:8000->80', '127.0.0.1:9000->80']      ← both published
volumes: data:/data kept;  /etc/app → conf-dev (and the base's :ro is gone)
with !override: ['127.0.0.1:9000->80'];  with !reset: build and depends_on absent

Appending is the trap. An override that "changes the port" adds a second one, and the spot-the-bug file ended up publishing 0.0.0.0:8080 next to 127.0.0.1:8000. And a volume override on the same target replaces the entry, flags included.

services:
  web:
    ports: !override
      - "127.0.0.1:9000:8080"

Rule Check every override with docker compose config, and use !override to replace lists and !reset to remove keys.

Why Compose appends lists, merges mappings and replaces scalars. Only the !override/!reset tags state the intent explicitly.

Trap After adding a dev override "to change the port", docker compose ps shows two port mappings, one of them on 0.0.0.0. The list was appended.

Rung 3 One base file, one file per environment

Put what every environment shares in compose.yaml. Put development extras in compose.override.yaml, so plain docker compose up on a laptop is the dev setup. Put production in compose.prod.yaml, used only with an explicit -f list, because an explicit list replaces the automatic override:

docker compose up -d --wait                                          # laptop: compose.yaml + compose.override.yaml
REGISTRY=localhost:5001 TAG=1.1.0 \
  docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d --wait   # server: no override, a released image

without REGISTRY:  error while interpolating services.web.image: required variable REGISTRY is missing a value: set REGISTRY
with TAG=1.1.0:    web Pulled … Healthy … Hello from Pantry (1.1.0). You are visitor #6.
HostConfig: memory=268435456 nanocpus=1000000000 log=json-file {"max-file":"3","max-size":"10m"}

The production file does what only production needs. build: !reset null means the server never builds: it pulls what CI built and scanned (D6). deploy.resources.limits are enforced by plain docker compose, not just Swarm (256 MiB and one CPU above). logging rotates json-file logs, which otherwise grow without limit. Two more facts were measured. --scale web=2 fails while a fixed host port is published (port is already allocated), so scaling needs a proxy in front. And down interpolates the files too: run it without REGISTRY and TAG and nothing is stopped.

Rule Keep compose.yaml shared, compose.override.yaml for development only, and production in a separate file always named with -f, with images by release tag (or digest), resource limits and log rotation.

Why The override file is loaded automatically wherever docker compose up runs without -f, including on a server where someone typed it from habit.

Trap Production shows the debug banner. The deploy script ran docker compose up -d in a checkout that contains compose.override.yaml, so the dev file was merged in. That is what the spot-the-bug project did: "DEBUG BUILD - do not use".

Rung 4 Profiles: services that start only when asked

A service with profiles: [tools] is ignored by up unless the profile is active. Use it for admin tools, debug containers, load generators and one-off jobs you do not want running all the time:

  redis-cli:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    profiles: [tools]

$ docker compose ps --services           → redis, web            (redis-cli not started)
$ docker compose --profile tools run --rm redis-cli GET visits    → 1
$ docker compose run --rm redis-cli GET visits                    → 6   (run names it, so its profile is enabled)
$ docker compose config --profiles       → tools

COMPOSE_PROFILES=tools,debug activates profiles from the environment. A service without profiles: always starts, so do not make a core service depend on a profiled one.

Rule Put optional services in profiles and run them with docker compose run --rm <service>.

Why Profiles keep the default up to the services the application needs, while the tools stay defined, versioned and on the same networks.

Trap docker compose up fails with service "app" depends on undefined service "debug": invalid compose project. A core service depends_on a profiled one, which does not exist while its profile is off.

Rung 5 include and extends

include: pulls another Compose project fragment (services, volumes, networks, secrets) into this one. Relative paths in the included file resolve against its directory, so a team can own redis/compose.yaml independently:

include:
  - redis/compose.yaml            # services, volumes and secrets from another file, with its own relative paths

extends: copies one service's definition into another, then merges local keys over it, which is useful for a family of similar services (workers on different queues):

services:
  worker:
    extends: {file: common.yaml, service: worker-base}
    command: ["echo", "worker"]
    environment: {QUEUE: emails}

→ cap_drop: [ALL], LOG_LEVEL: info, QUEUE: emails, image: alpine:3.20

The difference: include adds whole resources and refuses to redefine them (services.redis conflicts with imported resource), and extends builds one service from another. Neither is a substitute for override files, which change the same services per environment.

Rule Use include to compose a project from fragments owned elsewhere, extends for services that share most of their definition, and override files for per-environment changes.

Why Each mechanism merges at a different level (project, service, environment), with its own path resolution and conflict rules.

Trap A volume path in an included file "does not exist". It was written relative to the main project, but include resolves it relative to the included file's own directory.

Rung 6 Extension fields and YAML anchors

Top-level keys starting with x- are ignored by Compose, which makes them a place to define reusable blocks. YAML anchors (&name) and merge keys (<<: *name) do the reuse:

x-hardening: &hardening
  read_only: true
  tmpfs: ["/tmp:size=16m"]
  cap_drop: [ALL]
  security_opt: ["no-new-privileges:true"]

services:
  web:
    <<: *hardening
    environment:
      <<: *redis-client
      GREETING: ${GREETING:-Hello from Pantry}

Anchors are plain YAML, resolved when the file is parsed. They work inside one file only (not across -f files or include), and <<: merges mappings, not lists. A list you write next to it replaces the anchored list.

Rule Define repeated blocks (hardening, logging, client settings) once under x- keys and merge them with <<: *anchor.

Why One definition means one place to change, and Compose ignores x- keys, so they cost nothing.

Trap An anchor "does nothing" in the override file. Anchors do not cross files. Repeat the block, or move the setting into the base file.

Rung 7 Secrets (and configs) as files

Compose secrets: mounts a value as a file at /run/secrets/<name>, outside docker inspect's environment listing and outside docker compose config output. The app reads the file. Pantry reads REDIS_PASSWORD_FILE:

secrets:
  redis_password:
    file: ./secrets/redis_password.txt   # git-ignored; bind-mounted read-only

mkdir -p secrets && openssl rand -hex 16 > secrets/redis_password.txt && chmod 600 secrets/redis_password.txt

Compose can also take a secret's value from an environment variable (environment: REDIS_PASSWORD), but it does so by copying the value into the container's filesystem before start. On a hardened service that fails:

secrets: … environment: REDIS_PASSWORD  +  read_only: true
Error response from daemon: container rootfs is marked read-only          (also with a tmpfs at /run/secrets)
secrets: … file: ./secrets/redis_password.txt  → works

Getting the value into a program that wants it as a flag needs one more step, because flags are visible in ps, docker top and docker inspect. The Redis fragment writes the password into a config file on a tmpfs and starts redis-server /tmp/redis.conf, and clients use REDISCLI_AUTH instead of -a. Afterwards the password appeared 0 times in docker top output and 0 times in docker compose config. configs: work the same way for non-secret files (mounted at a path you choose). On Linux the bind-mounted file keeps its host owner and mode, so a 600 file owned by you is unreadable by UID 10001. Docker Desktop hides this. Make it readable by the container's GID.

Rule Pass secrets as secrets: files read by the app (*_FILE variables), keep the files out of git, and never put a secret's value in environment:, command: or the Compose file.

Why Files under /run/secrets do not appear in the environment, inspect output or process lists, and a file-sourced secret is a bind mount, which works with read_only.

Trap A hardened service fails to start with container rootfs is marked read-only after secrets were added. The secret is sourced from environment:. Use file:.

Rung 8 develop.watch: edit, sync, restart, rebuild

develop.watch (with docker compose up --watch or docker compose watch) reacts to file changes without bind mounts:

    develop:
      watch:
        - action: sync+restart
          path: ../../pantry/app.py
          target: /app/app.py
        - action: rebuild
          path: ../../pantry/requirements.txt

The actions:

  • sync copies the changed file into the running container, for servers that reload by themselves.
  • sync+restart copies the file, then restarts the container, for servers like gunicorn that need a restart.
  • rebuild rebuilds the image and recreates the container, for dependency changes.

Unlike a bind mount, watch works with the image's own layout and ownership, and does not drag the host's node_modules or __pycache__ into the container.

It needs a writable target, so the dev override sets read_only: false. One more trap, found while testing this chapter on Compose 2.32:

Syncing and restarting service "web" after 1 changes were detected
Error handling changed files for service web: … getent unable to find entry "10001:10001" in passwd database

The copy resolves the container's user string, and uid:gid form is not a passwd entry. With user: "10001" in the override:

Syncing and restarting service "web" after 1 changes were detected
service "web" restarted
Hello from dev (dev). You are visitor #5. Edited live. Edited again. …

Rule Use develop.watch with sync, sync+restart and rebuild in the dev override instead of bind-mounting the source, and give watched services a plain numeric user.

Why Watch keeps the container's image-defined filesystem and copies only what changed, so dev runs the same layout as production.

Trap Saving a file does nothing, and the watch output shows an error copying files. The target is read-only, or the container user is in uid:gid form. Read the line after "Syncing".

Decide

You need Use
Dev-only settings compose.override.yaml (automatic)
Production settings compose.prod.yaml with an explicit -f list
A second copy on the same host -p <name> / COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME
Replace a list in an override !override
Drop a key in an override !reset
Optional tools profiles: + docker compose run --rm
A fragment owned by another team include:
Many similar services extends:
Repeated settings in one file x- + anchors
Passwords and keys secrets: with file: + *_FILE in the app
Live reload without bind mounts develop.watch
Several hosts, self-healing, rolling updates Kubernetes (the rest of this book)

Compose stops being enough at the last row. It runs one project on one Docker host. It does not restart unhealthy containers, does not move work when the host dies, and cannot roll out a new version without a gap. The Bridge chapter maps every key in this chapter to its Kubernetes counterpart.

The golden file

Pantry as a project: a shared base that includes the Redis fragment, uses anchors for hardening and client settings, a tools profile and a file secret; a dev override with watch; and a production file that runs a released image with limits and rotated logs.

mkdir -p secrets && openssl rand -hex 16 > secrets/redis_password.txt && chmod 600 secrets/redis_password.txt
docker compose up -d --wait                       # dev: Hello from dev (dev). …
docker compose --profile tools run --rm redis-cli GET visits
REGISTRY=localhost:5001 TAG=1.1.0 docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d --wait

Review checklist

Spot the bug

The project as committed, deployed with git pull && docker compose up -d.

# compose.yaml — deployed on the server with:  git pull && docker compose up -d
name: pantry
services:
  web:
    image: localhost:5001/pantry-manual:1.1.0
    container_name: pantry-web
    environment:
      REDIS_HOST: redis
      GREETING: Hello from Pantry
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8000:8080"
  redis:
    image: redis:7-alpine
    command: ["redis-server", "--appendonly", "yes"]
    volumes: [redis-data:/data]
volumes:
  redis-data:
---
# compose.override.yaml — "local development tweaks", committed next to it
services:
  web:
    environment:
      GREETING: DEBUG BUILD - do not use
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

This file has 4 problems.

Show answers
  1. The deploy command has no -f, so the server merged compose.override.yaml and served "DEBUG BUILD - do not use". Deploy with docker compose -f compose.yaml -f compose.prod.yaml up -d, and keep dev settings out of whatever the server loads.
  2. The override's ports list was appended, not substituted: 0.0.0.0:8080->8080/tcp, 127.0.0.1:8000->8080/tcp, and port 8080 answered from the LAN. Use ports: !override [...], and bind to 127.0.0.1.
  3. container_name: pantry-web makes the service impossible to scale ("Docker requires each container to have a unique name") and collides with any second copy. Remove it.
  4. The fixed name: pantry is shared by every checkout. Bringing up a staging copy on port 8100 recreated production's web container and used production's Redis (visitor #4). Give each copy its own -p.
